fizik-bilimine-giris.ozet: Try first, learn the name after. Run an experiment, measure, and turn the arrow yourself.

adimlar.metin: Let's begin with an experiment. A steel ball and a feather are released at the same moment in a tube with the air pumped out.

gorev.soru: Which one hits the ground first?

secenekler.neden: In a vacuum every object falls with the same acceleration, whatever its mass. Astronaut David Scott showed this on the Moon in 1971 with a hammer and a feather.
It feels as if the heavier one should land first. But without air, mass does not make the fall any faster.
Being light does not make the feather fall faster.

adimlar.metin: In everyday life the feather still falls slowly. Form a hypothesis, a prediction you can test: maybe air makes the difference. To test it, choose Air below.

gorev.ipucu: Choose “Air” below. The experiment replays on its own.
gorev.tamam: The ball was barely affected, but the feather slowed down. So air resistance makes the difference. Your hypothesis was confirmed by experiment.

adimlar.metin: You have rods that are 25 cm long. Line up enough rods to cover the table exactly.

gorev.tamam: The table is 6 rods long, which is 150 cm (1.5 m). With a 30 cm rod you would have counted 5. So the number depends on the unit. That is why a result is always written with a number and a unit, and everyone uses the same units, the SI units.

adimlar.metin: The SI has seven base quantities, and every other quantity is built from them. Look at the table.

gorev.soru: Why is speed (m/s) not in this table?

secenekler.yazi: It is derived from length and time
secenekler.neden: Speed is built from length (m) and time (s), and its unit is m/s. Quantities built from base quantities like this are called derived quantities.
Speed can be measured, and a car's speedometer does exactly that. Look at its unit: what is m/s made of?

secenekler.yazi: Speed is not part of the SI
secenekler.neden: Speed is part of the SI and its unit is m/s, but it is not a base quantity. Look at which two base quantities it is built from.

adimlar.metin: A runner runs 100 meters. Speed is the distance divided by the time. Change the time and make the runner's speed 10 m/s.

gorev.tamam: 100 m ÷ 10 s = 10 m/s. So the runner covers 10 m every second. The world's fastest sprinters run 100 meters in just under 10 seconds.

adimlar.metin: If I say "walk 3 km", you cannot tell where you will end up. The school is northeast of your home. Grab the arrow and turn it.

gorev.tamam: Walk 3 km northeast and now it is clear where you end up. Quantities that also need a direction, such as displacement, velocity and force, are called vector quantities.

kapanis: Physics studies matter, energy and how they interact through observation, experiment and mathematics.
A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested. A law tells you what happens, and a theory explains why.
To measure is to compare a quantity with a known unit. The result always has a number and a unit.
The SI has 7 base quantities. Other quantities, such as speed (m/s), are derived from them.
A scalar has no direction. A vector also needs a direction.

vektorler.ozet: Try first, learn the name after. Draw a vector, rotate and add, then split it into components.

adimlar.metin: θ is the angle the arrow makes with the +x axis (pointing right). Draw the vector with length 3 units and θ = 135°.

gorev.tamam: Since 135° = 90° + 45°, the arrow points up and to the left.

adimlar.metin: A is 3 units long and B is 4 units long. Rotate B and make the resultant exactly 5 units.

gorev.tamam: When A and B are perpendicular they form a right triangle, and R = √(3² + 4²) = 5. The magnitude of the resultant depends on the angle between the vectors. Adding the numbers is not enough.

adimlar.baslik: How big can the resultant be?
adimlar.metin: Turn B from 0° to 180° and watch how the resultant changes.

gorev.soru: In what range does the resultant of two vectors of 3 and 4 units stay?

secenekler.neden: For the resultant to be zero, the vectors would need equal lengths. Set B to 180° and look.
It is largest in the same direction (3 + 4 = 7) and smallest in opposite directions (4 − 3 = 1). The resultant always lies between |A − B| and A + B.
Set B to 0°. The resultant becomes 7, which is more than 4.

adimlar.metin: Make a vector twice as long as A but pointing the opposite way.

gorev.tamam: This vector is −2A. It is twice as long and points the opposite way.

adimlar.metin: V is 10 units long. Change the angle and make the vertical component 5.

gorev.tamam: Since sin30° = 0.5, V<sub>y</sub> = 10 × 0.5 = 5. The horizontal component is V<sub>x</sub> = 10 × cos30° ≈ 8.66.

adimlar.metin: You walked 3 steps east. How many steps north must you walk to be exactly 5 steps from where you started?

gorev.tamam: √(3² + 4²) = 5. You walked 7 steps in total, but your displacement is 5 steps. The total length of your path (the distance) is a scalar, while displacement is a vector.

kapanis: A scalar quantity is given by a number and a unit (mass, temperature, time). A vector quantity also needs a direction (force, velocity, displacement).
For vectors added head to tail, the resultant is the arrow from the first tail to the last head. The resultant always lies between |A − B| and A + B.
The length of kA is |k| times the length of A, and if k is negative the direction is reversed. A − B means A + (−B).
The components are Vx = V·cosθ and Vy = V·sinθ. The magnitude is V = √(Vx² + Vy²).

bir-boyutta-hareket.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Drive the car, drag the graph, and throw the ball.

adimlar.metin: Drag the car to the yellow flag.

gorev.tamam: The car is 30 m from the start, so its position is x = 30 m. Position is always given relative to a starting point.

adimlar.metin: You can measure a trip in two ways. One is where you started and where you ended up. The other is how far you traveled in total.

gorev.soru: The car will go 40 m forward, then 30 m back. What do you think its displacement (Δx) is, in meters?

secenekler.neden: Displacement only looks at the first and last positions, so Δx = 10 − 0 = +10 m. The total length traveled is the distance, and it is 40 + 30 = 70 m.
70 m is the total length the car traveled. That is the distance.
−30 m is only the displacement on the way back. Don't forget the first 40 m.

adimlar.metin: The camera takes one frame every second. A moves 5 m each second. Set B's velocity and press play. Make the two cars travel side by side.

gorev.tamam: Both cars move 5 m each second, so v = Δx / Δt = 25 m / 5 s = 5 m/s. Equal velocities mean equally spaced frames.

adimlar.metin: As the car moves, it plots its position on the graph at every moment. Pick two different velocities and play both.

gorev.soru: What does the faster car's line look like?

secenekler.neden: The fast car covers more ground each second, so its line rises faster. The slope of a position-time graph is the velocity.
Look at the graphs. Which line is higher at second 5?
The two lines don't end at the same place. Which one ends higher?

adimlar.metin: The car starts from rest and steps on the gas. Pick an acceleration and press play.

gorev.soru: Which of these strips looks like the frames taken each second?

secenekler.yazi: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 20" class="ad-serit" aria-hidden="true"><line x1="6" x2="194" y1="10" y2="10" stroke="var(--line-2)" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="6" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="53" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="100" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="147" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="194" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/></svg>
secenekler.neden: Equal gaps mean constant velocity. A car that speeds up covers more ground each second.

secenekler.yazi: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 20" class="ad-serit" aria-hidden="true"><line x1="6" x2="194" y1="10" y2="10" stroke="var(--line-2)" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="6" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="18" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="53" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="112" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="194" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/></svg>
secenekler.neden: As the velocity grows, the car covers more ground each second, so the frames spread apart. The velocity-time graph also rises as a straight line.

secenekler.yazi: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 20" class="ad-serit" aria-hidden="true"><line x1="6" x2="194" y1="10" y2="10" stroke="var(--line-2)" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="6" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="88" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="147" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="182" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/><circle cx="194" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="var(--ink)"/></svg>
secenekler.neden: If the gaps shrink, the car is slowing down. How did the frames above spread?

adimlar.metin: The car moves at a constant 5 m/s. Drag the handle on the graph to move time forward and bring the car to the flag.

gorev.tamam: The car traveled 20 m in 4 s. The shaded rectangle also has an area of 5 · 4 = 20. So the area under a velocity-time graph gives the distance traveled.

adimlar.metin: Now the car starts from rest and speeds up by 2 m/s each second. Drag the handle and bring the car to the flag at 16 m.

gorev.tamam: After 4 s the velocity was 8 m/s. The shaded triangle has an area of ½ · 8 · 4 = 16 m. The area rule also works for a car that speeds up.

adimlar.metin: In a tube with the air pumped out, a 5 kg cannonball and a 1 g feather will be dropped at the same moment.

gorev.soru: Which one hits the ground first?

secenekler.neden: The cannonball is pulled with a larger force, but its mass is larger by the same factor. So its acceleration is the same as the feather's.
What slows a feather in air is air resistance. This tube has no air.
Without air, every object falls with the same acceleration. Both fell 20 m in 2 s. The gap between the marks grew each time, so they sped up as they fell.

adimlar.metin: Drag the velocity arrow upward to choose the launch speed, then press play. Make the ball rise to exactly 20 m.

gorev.tamam: The ball thrown at 20 m/s slowed by 10 m/s each second, stopped after 2 s, and reached 20 m. Then it came back in the same time, at the same speed.

adimlar.baslik: Read the motion from a graph
adimlar.metin: This time the graph is ready. Press play and watch the car. What happens in the yellow region?

gorev.soru: What is the car doing between seconds 2 and 4, where the graph is flat?

secenekler.neden: The position does not change, and x stays at 30 m. A horizontal line has zero slope, so the velocity is zero. In the last part the line goes down, so the car is coming back.
A car moving at constant velocity changes position every second, so its line is sloped. Is x changing here?
The position graph of a car that speeds up is a curve that gets steeper. Press play and watch the car.

kapanis: Position is where you are relative to the start. Displacement is Δx = xfinal − xinitial.
Distance is the total length traveled. If you turn back, the distance is larger than Δx.

Velocity is displacement divided by time (v = Δx / Δt), and it is the slope of the position-time graph. Total distance divided by time is called speed. On a trip where you turn back, the two are different.
Acceleration is the change in velocity each second. For a car that speeds up, the frames spread apart.
If the position-time graph is flat, the car is stopped. If it goes down, the car is moving back.

bagil-hareket.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Switch the observer, and look at velocity from cars and from a boat.

adimlar.metin: The train moves at 20 m/s relative to the ground. Switch the observer. Look first from the platform, then from the seat of the friend on the train.

gorev.soru: Is the passenger on the train moving?

secenekler.neden: That is true for the person on the platform. But relative to the friend on the train, the passenger is not moving at all.

secenekler.yazi: It depends on who is looking
secenekler.neden: The passenger moves at 20 m/s relative to the platform and is at rest relative to the friend. The observer you measure motion from is called the reference frame. A velocity is incomplete without its reference.
That is true for the friend. But how does the person on the platform see the passenger?

adimlar.metin: A moves east at 90 km/h. Set B's velocity so that the driver of A sees B at rest.

gorev.tamam: 90 − 90 = 0. Cars moving in the same direction at the same speed see each other at rest.

adimlar.metin: Now let B move west. Make the driver of A see B moving west at 150 km/h.

gorev.tamam: The velocity of B relative to A is −60 − 90 = −150 km/h, which is 150 km/h toward the west. Speeds in opposite directions add.

adimlar.metin: A 24 m escalator moves up at 1 m/s, so if you stand on it you reach the top in 24 s. If you walk at 0.5 m/s on a stopped escalator, the climb takes 48 s.

gorev.soru: If you walk up the moving escalator, how many seconds does it take to reach the top?

secenekler.neden: Both you and the escalator are going up. Together you are faster than either one alone.
Both the escalator and you are going up. So you must be faster than either one alone.

Your velocity relative to the ground is 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 m/s, so the climb takes 24 / 1.5 = 16 s. Velocities add, times do not. If you walked the other way, your velocity would be 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 m/s and the climb would take 48 s.

adimlar.metin: The boat moves at 4 m/s relative to the water, with its bow pointed straight across. The river is 80 m wide. Change the current and press play at least twice.

gorev.soru: When the current got faster, what happened to the crossing time?

secenekler.neden: The current runs parallel to the bank. So it does not slow the motion straight across.
The current only pushes the boat sideways. It does not bring it closer to the other bank.

The crossing time is the width divided by the velocity perpendicular to the bank: 80 / 4 = 20 s. The current does not change the time. It only increases the drift. With a 3 m/s current the drift is 3 · 20 = 60 m.

adimlar.metin: The river is 60 m wide, the boat's speed is 5 m/s, and the current is 3 m/s. Turn the bow upstream and land the boat directly opposite. Set the angle, then press play.

gorev.ipucu: The boat's upstream component must exactly balance the current (3 m/s).
gorev.tamam: At about 37° (sin37° = 0.6), the upstream component is 5 · 0.6 = 3 m/s and balances the current. The component perpendicular to the bank is 5 · 0.8 = 4 m/s, so the crossing takes 60 / 4 = 15 s.

adimlar.metin: With no wind, rain falls straight down at 8 m/s. Speed the car up until the drops come at 10 m/s relative to someone in the car.

gorev.tamam: Relative to someone in the car, the rain comes at 8 m/s downward and 6 m/s backward. Its speed is √(8² + 6²) = 10 m/s. For the angle from the vertical, tanθ = 6/8 = 0.75, so θ ≈ 37°.

kapanis: Velocity is measured relative to an observer. A velocity is incomplete without its reference.
Relative velocity is the object's velocity minus the observer's velocity, as vectors. Velocities in the same direction subtract, and those in opposite directions add.
Velocity relative to the ground is the velocity relative to the vehicle plus the vehicle's velocity relative to the ground. Velocities add, times do not.
On a river, crossing time = width / velocity perpendicular to the bank. The current does not change the time. It carries the boat downstream.
From a vehicle, rain looks slanted because of its relative velocity.

newton-yasalari.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Pull the cloth, push the box, and push off on a skateboard.

adimlar.metin: The net force is the sum of all the forces acting on an object. The person on the left pushes to the right with 30 N. Set the force of the person on the right and make the net force zero.

gorev.tamam: 30 N acts to the right and 30 N to the left, so the net force is 0. The forces are there, but the box's velocity does not change. The first law explains why.

adimlar.metin: You are going to pull the tablecloth away in one quick move.

gorev.soru: What happens to the plates when you pull the cloth quickly?

secenekler.yazi: They slide along with the cloth
secenekler.neden: The cloth can only pull the plates through friction. When you pull very fast, that force lasts a very short time.

secenekler.yazi: They stay in place on the table
secenekler.neden: Plates at rest stay at rest. Friction acts for such a short time that their velocity hardly changes. This is called inertia.
No upward force acts on the plates.

adimlar.metin: Acceleration tells you how much the velocity changes each second. Push the 10 kg cart so that its acceleration is 2 m/s², then press play.

gorev.tamam: a = 20 N / 10 kg = 2 m/s². The velocity grows 2 m/s each second, and the cart travels ½ · 2 · 2² = 4 m in 2 s.

adimlar.metin: The force now stays at 20 N. Change the cart's mass and press play with at least two different masses.

gorev.soru: With the same force, what happens to the acceleration when the mass doubles?

secenekler.neden: A heavy cart is harder to speed up. Compare the accelerations for 10 kg and 20 kg.
Since a = F / m, changing m changes a.
With 20 N, the acceleration is 2 m/s² at 10 kg and 1 m/s² at 20 kg. Since a = F / m, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

adimlar.metin: You are standing on a skateboard and your mass is 60 kg. You are going to push your 30 kg brother with a force of 60 N.

gorev.soru: Who rolls away when you push?

secenekler.yazi: Both of you, in opposite directions
secenekler.neden: Your brother pushes you back with the same magnitude (60 N) in the opposite direction. The forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel. Your brother has half your mass, so he moves away twice as fast (a = F / m).
Your brother also puts a force of the same magnitude on you. So you roll backward too.
The force you put on your brother makes him move too.

adimlar.metin: Take the 60 kg astronaut to the Moon. This scene uses real values: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth and g ≈ 1.62 m/s² on the Moon.

gorev.tamam: The mass is still 60 kg, but the weight dropped from 60 × 9.8 ≈ 588 N to 60 × 1.62 ≈ 97 N.

adimlar.metin: A box sits on the floor. μs = 0.5, μk = 0.3, and g = 10 m/s². Change the push and the mass. The force arrows, velocity, and acceleration update right away. Find the answers below yourself.

bulgular.yazi: Find the smallest push that makes the 20 kg box slide.
bulgular.tamam: The limit of static friction is μs·N = 0.5 × 200 = 100 N. When the push went above that, the box slid. Now kinetic friction acts, and μk·N = 0.3 × 200 = 60 N.

bulgular.yazi: While the box is sliding, lower the push to 60 N. Watch its velocity.
bulgular.tamam: The push equals kinetic friction. The net force is zero, so the box moves at constant velocity (first law). Starting the motion took more than 100 N, but 60 N is enough to keep it going.

bulgular.yazi: Set the mass to 40 kg and find the smallest push that makes the box slide again.
bulgular.tamam: When the mass doubled, N became 400 N and the limit also doubled to μs·N = 200 N. Friction is proportional to the normal force.

kapanis: First law: if the net force is zero, the velocity does not change. Being at rest is also constant velocity (v = 0).
Second law: Fnet = m·a. With the same force, doubling the mass cuts the acceleration in half. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different objects. That is why they do not cancel.
Weight is W = m·g (N). Mass (kg) is the same everywhere.
For an object at rest, friction balances the push up to μs·N. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N.

iki-boyutta-hareket.baslik: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles
iki-boyutta-hareket.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Drop the balls, throw a stone off a cliff, and set the angle.

adimlar.metin: From the same height, you will drop one ball and throw the other horizontally. There is no air resistance.

gorev.soru: Which one hits the ground first?

secenekler.neden: Its shorter path does not matter. Only gravity sets the vertical motion.
Horizontal velocity does not speed up the fall. Both fall with the same g.
The two balls are at the same height at every moment. Horizontal velocity neither speeds up nor slows down the fall. Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.

adimlar.metin: You will throw a stone horizontally from a 19.6 m cliff, and it will land after 2 s. Set the speed and land the stone on the flag 40 m away.

gorev.tamam: The fall took 2 s, because h = ½·g·t² gives 19.6 = 4.9·t² and t = 2 s. In that time the stone moved x = 20 × 2 = 40 m horizontally.

adimlar.metin: Throw the stone from the same cliff at two or more different speeds. Check how long each throw takes.

gorev.soru: When you throw the stone faster, what happens to the time of flight?

secenekler.neden: The stone goes farther, but not in more time. Look at the times.
Every throw took 2 s. The time of flight only depends on the height: t = √(2h / g). The speed only changes how far the stone goes.
Horizontal velocity does not speed up the fall.

adimlar.metin: You launch the ball at 20 m/s and an angle of 60°.

gorev.soru: What is the ball's speed at the top, in m/s?

secenekler.neden: Only the vertical velocity is zero at the top. The ball is still moving horizontally.
That is the launch speed. The vertical velocity dropped as the ball rose.
v<sub>x</sub> = 20 × cos60° = 10 m/s never changes. At the top v<sub>y</sub> = 0, so the speed equals v<sub>x</sub>. It is not zero.

adimlar.metin: This is a projectile lab. Change the angle and the speed, or drag the tip of the barrel. The path, range, and maximum height update right away. There is no air resistance. Find the answers below yourself.

bulgular.yazi: With the speed at 20 m/s, find the angle that sends the ball farthest.
bulgular.tamam: At 45° the range is R = v0²·sin2θ / g = 400 × 1 / 9.8 ≈ 41 m, and that is the largest range. With no air resistance and a landing at launch level, the longest range comes at 45°.

bulgular.yazi: At the same speed, launch first at 30°, then at 60°. Compare the ranges.
bulgular.tamam: The range is about 35 m in both cases. For angles that add up to 90°, sin2θ is the same (sin60° = sin120°). The ball launched at 60° rises higher and flies longer, but it is slower horizontally.

bulgular.yazi: At 45°, set the speed first to 10, then to 20 m/s. How many times larger is the range?
bulgular.tamam: The range is about 10.2 m at 10 m/s and about 40.8 m at 20 m/s. When the speed doubled, the range became 4 times larger, because R = v0²·sin2θ / g grows with the square of the speed.

kapanis: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Horizontally the velocity is constant, and vertically the acceleration is g.
In a horizontal launch, the time of flight only depends on the height: t = √(2h / g). The horizontal distance is x = v0·t.
In a launch at an angle, vx = v0·cosθ is constant and vy = v0·sinθ − g·t. At the top vy = 0, but the object's speed equals vx.
The range is R = v0²·sin2θ / g. Without air, the largest range is at 45°, and 30° and 60° give the same range.
In reality, air resistance lowers the range and the height. The angle for the longest range is usually a little less than 45°.

cembersel-hareket.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Watch the ball go around, compare speeds on a Ferris wheel, and take a curve without skidding.

adimlar.metin: The ball goes around the circle at constant speed. The velocity arrow is always tangent to the circle, and since its direction changes, the ball is accelerating.

gorev.soru: Which way does this acceleration point?

secenekler.neden: A tangent acceleration would change the speed. But the speed is constant.
An acceleration that changes only the direction, not the speed, is perpendicular to the velocity and always points toward the center (red arrow). It is called centripetal acceleration.
An outward acceleration would move the ball away from the circle. Which way must the acceleration point to bend the ball's path around the circle?

adimlar.metin: Frequency is the number of turns per second, measured in hertz. Set the washing machine drum to 25 Hz.

gorev.tamam: 1500 turns per minute is 1500 / 60 = 25 turns per second, so f = 25 Hz. One turn takes T = 1/25 = 0.04 s.

adimlar.metin: The Ferris wheel makes one turn every 20 seconds. You are in the outer seat, 8 m from the center. Your friend is in the inner seat, 4 m from the center.

gorev.soru: Which of you moves faster?

secenekler.yazi: We move at the same speed
secenekler.neden: You both go around in the same time, so your angular speed is the same. But the outer seat covers more distance.
In one turn the outer seat travels 2π·8 ≈ 50 m and the inner seat about 25 m, and both do it in 20 s. Twice the distance in the same time means twice the speed.
The seat near the center traces a smaller circle and covers less distance in the same time.

adimlar.metin: You whirl a stone on a string in a horizontal plane, and we are looking from above. The string will break when the stone is at its northernmost point, moving east.

gorev.soru: Where does the stone go when the string breaks?

secenekler.neden: Once the force pulling toward the center is gone, the first law says the stone keeps the velocity it has and moves straight along the tangent. A hammer thrower lets go at exactly this kind of moment.
No force pushes outward. Centrifugal force is a misconception.
The string tension was what kept the stone on the circle. Without it, the path becomes straight.

adimlar.metin: The centripetal force needed is F = m·v²/r. A 1000 kg car is on a curve with a radius of 50 m. Change the speed and make the force 8000 N.

gorev.tamam: 1000 · 20² / 50 = 8000 N. When the speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s, the force needed becomes four times larger. This is not a new force. Here, friction between the tires and the road supplies it.

adimlar.metin: The maximum safe speed on a curve is √(μ·g·r), where μ is the surface's coefficient of friction. Your car will take a 50 m curve at 15 m/s. Choose the road surface and take the curve without skidding.

gorev.tamam: At μ = 0.5 the limit is √(0.5 · 9.8 · 50) ≈ 15.7 m/s, so 15 m/s is safe. In rain μ drops, and so does the limit. That is why you slow down on a wet road.

adimlar.metin: A skater spins with arms out, and there is no external torque. Pulling the arms in to the body will cut the moment of inertia I in half.

gorev.soru: What happens when the skater pulls the arms in?

secenekler.neden: If I gets smaller while L stays constant, ω must get larger.

secenekler.yazi: The skater spins twice as fast
secenekler.neden: The product I·ω, the angular momentum, stays constant: 4 · 2 = 2 · 4. When I is cut in half, ω doubles.
If the spin stayed the same, cutting I in half would cut L in half too. But L cannot change without an external torque.

kapanis: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant, but the direction of the velocity changes. So the object is accelerating, and the acceleration always points toward the center.
f = 1/T and v = ω·r = 2πr/T. On a rotating object ω is the same at every point, while v grows with the radius.
F = m·v²/r is not a new force. It is the net force toward the center. Tension, friction, or gravity supplies it.
When the force is gone, the object moves straight along the tangent. On a level curve the safe speed is v ≤ √(μ·g·r).
With no external torque, angular momentum L = I·ω is conserved.

kutle-cekimi.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Tune gravity with mass and distance, put the ball into orbit, and cut the elevator cable.

adimlar.metin: Double the distance. Then set B's mass and bring the force back to F₀.

gorev.tamam: When the distance doubles, the force drops to one part in 2² = 4. Making the mass 4 times larger brings the force back to F₀. This is called the inverse-square law.
gorev.ipucu: First set the distance to 2 and see what fraction the force drops to.

adimlar.baslik: The apple pulls on Earth too
adimlar.metin: A 100 g apple falls from a tree. Earth pulls on the apple with about 1 N.

gorev.soru: How hard does the apple pull on Earth?

secenekler.neden: Every object with mass attracts. Being small does not make the force disappear.
Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The forces are equal. What is small is Earth's acceleration, not the force.

adimlar.baslik: g gets smaller as you rise
adimlar.metin: An 80 kg astronaut rises above the ground. Bring the astronaut's weight down to about 87 N.

gorev.tamam: At 12 800 km up, r = 3R and g drops to one part in 3² = 9 (about 1.09 m/s²). The weight is 784 / 9 ≈ 87 N. The mass is still 80 kg.
gorev.ipucu: For the weight to drop to one ninth, the distance from the center must triple.

adimlar.metin: Watch the planet for one full trip around its elliptical orbit.

gorev.soru: When is the planet fastest?

secenekler.yazi: Its speed is always the same
secenekler.neden: Close to the Sun, gravity is stronger and the planet speeds up.
It is slowest at aphelion. It has to move slowly so that the area swept in equal times stays the same.
Close to the Sun, the radius is short. To sweep the same area in the same time, the planet has to move faster.

adimlar.metin: A ball thrown horizontally from a mountaintop both falls and moves forward. If you throw it fast enough, the surface curves away beneath it. Put the ball into orbit.

gorev.tamam: A ball thrown at about 7.9 km/s goes around Earth. A satellite is always falling too, but it keeps missing Earth. Gravity acts as the centripetal force, and v = √(GM/r).
gorev.ipucu: Raise the speed a little above 7.9 km/s and press play.

adimlar.metin: If you raise the speed even more, the orbit stretches out. Free the ball from Earth's gravity.

gorev.tamam: The escape velocity from Earth's surface is about 11.2 km/s, which is √2 times the orbital speed (7.9 × 1.41). An object thrown at this speed never comes back.
gorev.ipucu: Escape velocity is about 1.41 times the orbital speed.

adimlar.metin: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator, and the scale reads 588 N. Cut the cable and press play.

gorev.tamam: The person and the scale fall freely together, and the scale reads 0. Gravity is still there. It is the very reason they are falling.

kapanis: Any two masses attract each other, and F = G·m₁·m₂ / r². When the distance doubles, the force drops to one quarter.
Gravitational forces are equal and opposite. The apple also pulls on Earth with 1 N.
Since g = GM/r², it gets smaller as you rise. At r = 2R, g is one quarter of 9.8.
Planets sweep equal areas in equal times and speed up near the Sun.
Orbital speed is about 7.9 km/s and escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s. Satellites and astronauts are always falling.

is-enerji-guc.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Change the angle of the rope, drop the ball, and run up the stairs.

adimlar.metin: Work is the part of the force along the motion times the distance. You pull a box 5 m with a force of 40 N. Set the angle of the rope and make the work 100 J.

gorev.tamam: W = 40 · 5 · cos60° = 200 · 0.5 = 100 J. As the angle grows, the share of the force along the motion shrinks, and at 90° it is zero.

adimlar.metin: You walk along a level road at constant speed, holding a heavy bag. Your arm holds the bag upward, while the bag moves horizontally. So θ = 90°.

gorev.soru: How much work does your arm do on the bag?

secenekler.neden: Getting tired does not mean doing physical work. What is cos90°?
For negative work, the force must oppose the motion, as friction does. Here the force is perpendicular to the motion.
cos90° = 0. Your tiredness comes from the energy used inside your muscles, not from work transferred to the bag.

adimlar.metin: A 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s, and its kinetic energy is 50 000 J. Set the speed and make the kinetic energy 9 times larger.

gorev.tamam: At 30 m/s the kinetic energy is ½ · 1000 · 30² = 450 000 J. The speed went up 3 times, and the energy went up 3² = 9 times. That is why a fast vehicle is so much harder to stop.

adimlar.metin: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m, and its potential energy is 2 · 9.8 · 5 = 98 J. Only gravity does work on it.

gorev.soru: What is the ball's kinetic energy, in J, as it touches the ground?

secenekler.neden: The ball is fastest as it touches the ground, so its kinetic energy is largest there.
That is the value halfway down.
At the ground the potential energy is zero, and all of the lost 98 J has become kinetic energy. Since ½ · 2 · v² = 98 J, the ball hits the ground at about 9.9 m/s.

adimlar.metin: You release a skater from the edge of the ramp (g = 10 m/s²). Change the height, the mass, and the friction. The bar below shows how the energy changes form. Find out the following for yourself.

bulgular.yazi: On the frictionless ramp, find the height that makes the speed at the bottom 10 m/s.
bulgular.tamam: Since m·g·h = ½·m·v², v = √(2gh) = √(2·10·5) = 10 m/s. The skater rises to 5 m again on the other side, because KE + PE always stays the same.

bulgular.yazi: At 5 m, set the mass to 40 and then to 80 kg. Does the speed at the bottom change?
bulgular.tamam: The speed did not change (10 m/s), because m appears on both sides and cancels. But the energy doubled, from 2000 J to 4000 J.

bulgular.yazi: Turn friction on and watch until the skater stops. Where did the energy go?
bulgular.tamam: The mechanical energy (KE + PE) decreased, but the length of the bar did not change. The missing part turned into heat. Energy is never destroyed; it only changes form.

adimlar.metin: Power is work divided by time. On the same stairs, a 50 kg person climbs 3 m and does about 1470 J of work. Set the climbing time and make the power 210 W.

gorev.tamam: 1470 / 7 = 210 W. If the same work is done in less time, the power goes up. The 1 kWh on an electricity bill is 3.6 million J.

adimlar.baslik: The spring and the F–x graph
adimlar.metin: The spring constant is k = 200 N/m, and the energy stored in the spring is ½·k·x². Stretch the spring and store 4 J of energy in it.

gorev.tamam: At x = 0.2 m the force is F = 200 · 0.2 = 40 N, and the area of the triangle is ½ · 0.2 · 40 = 4 J. The extension doubled (from 10 cm to 20 cm), while the energy became 4 times larger (from 1 J to 4 J).

kapanis: Work is W = F·d·cosθ, and its unit is the joule. If the force is perpendicular to the motion or the object does not move, the work is zero.
Kinetic energy is KE = ½·m·v², and when the speed doubles the energy becomes 4 times larger. Potential energy is PE = m·g·h.
If only gravity does work, KE + PE stays constant. Friction turns part of the mechanical energy into heat, but the total energy is still conserved.
Power is P = W / t, and its unit is the watt. If the same work is done in less time, the power goes up.
The area under a force–extension graph gives the work. The energy stored in a spring is ½·k·x².

basit-makineler.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Balance the lever, lift a load with a block and tackle, and change the gear.

adimlar.metin: A 400 N load is 0.5 m from the pivot. The bar balances when force times distance is equal on both sides of the pivot. Balance the bar with the force you apply 2 m away.

gorev.tamam: 400 · 0.5 = 100 · 2 = 200 N·m. The effort arm is 4 times the load arm, so the force is 4 times smaller. That means the advantage is dF / dW = 4.

adimlar.metin: The order of the pivot (P), the load (W), and the effort (F) sets the type of lever. The item in the middle tells you which arm can be longer.

gorev.soru: Which one loses force (advantage less than 1)?

secenekler.neden: With the pivot in the middle, the advantage depends on the lengths of the arms and can also be greater than 1.
With the load in the middle, the effort arm is always longer than the load arm. So the advantage is greater than 1.
With the effort in the middle, the effort arm is always shorter than the load arm, and the advantage is less than 1. In return, the tip moves farther.

adimlar.baslik: Pulleys and the block and tackle
adimlar.metin: Change the number of rope strands carrying the movable block. Lift the 400 N load with 100 N.

gorev.tamam: 4 rope strands share the load, and 400 / 4 = 100 N. But when the load rises 1 m, you pull 4 m of rope. You gain in force and lose in distance. The work is still 400 J.

adimlar.metin: You will raise a 600 N crate by 1 m using a ramp. Make the ramp longer and bring the force needed down to 150 N.

gorev.tamam: 600 · 1 / 4 = 150 N. The ramp is 4 times longer, so the force is 4 times smaller. The work is always 600 J. A machine does not reduce the work, it only makes it easier.

adimlar.metin: The front gear has 48 teeth. Make the wheel turn 4 times for each turn of the pedal. Choose the rear gear and press play.

gorev.tamam: Since 48 / 12 = 4, the wheel makes 4 turns. If the wheel's circumference is 2 m, the bike travels 8 m per pedal turn. The bike is fast, but pedaling gets harder.

adimlar.metin: A real ramp has friction. Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to work input. Raising a 600 N load by 1 m on a 5 m ramp took a force of 150 N.

gorev.soru: What is the efficiency of this ramp, in percent?

secenekler.neden: Efficiency cannot exceed 100%. You divided the work input by the useful work. Do the reverse.
The useful work is 600 · 1 = 600 J, and the work input is 150 · 5 = 750 J. The efficiency is 600 / 750 = 80%. The remaining 150 J turned into heat.
20% is the part that goes into heat. Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to work input.

kapanis: Mechanical advantage is W / F. What you gain in force you lose in distance, and in an ideal machine the work does not change.
For a balanced lever F·dF = W·dW. With tweezers the effort is in the middle, and the advantage is less than 1.
The advantage is 1 for a fixed pulley and 2 for a movable pulley. For a block and tackle it equals the number of rope strands (n) carrying the load.
For an inclined plane F·L = W·h. For gears n₁·r₁ = n₂·r₂.
Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to work input, and in a real machine it is below 100%.

momentum.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Match the momenta, bounce the ball, and crash the carts.

adimlar.metin: Momentum is mass × velocity. A 4000 kg truck moves at 5 m/s. Set the speed of the 1000 kg car so that their momenta are equal.

gorev.tamam: 1000 · 20 = 4000 · 5 = 20 000 kg·m/s. If the mass is 4 times smaller, the speed must be 4 times larger. That is why a slow truck is hard to stop.

adimlar.baslik: A ball bouncing off a wall
adimlar.metin: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s. First let it stick, then let it bounce back. Play both cases and compare the change in momentum.

gorev.soru: When the ball bounces back at the same speed, what is the size of the change in momentum, in kg·m/s?

secenekler.neden: The speed is the same, but the direction reversed. Momentum is a vector.
That is the case where the ball sticks. When it bounces, the velocity goes from +10 to −10.
Δp = 0.2·(−10) − 0.2·10 = −4: the size is 4 kg·m/s, twice that of sticking. The wall gives the ball twice the impulse.

adimlar.metin: A 70 kg driver stops from 15 m/s, and Δp is always 1050 N·s. Make the stopping time longer and bring the force below 10 000 N.

gorev.tamam: The area under the graph, the impulse, is always 1050 N·s. As the time gets longer, the rectangle spreads out and its height, the force, gets smaller. At 150 ms the force is 1050 / 0.15 = 7000 N.

adimlar.metin: This collision is elastic. So kinetic energy is conserved along with momentum. The 1 kg cart A, moving at 4 m/s, will hit the 1 kg cart B at rest.

gorev.soru: What happens after the collision?

secenekler.neden: That happens when the carts stick together, and then kinetic energy decreases. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved.

secenekler.yazi: A bounces back, B moves slowly
secenekler.neden: That happens when a light object hits a heavy one. Here the masses are equal.

secenekler.yazi: A stops, B moves at 4 m/s
secenekler.neden: Only this way are momentum (4 kg·m/s) and KE (8 J) both conserved. With equal masses, the velocities swap.

adimlar.metin: Now the carts stick together when they collide, so m1·v1 = (m1 + m2)·v. Choose the mass of B and press play. Make the common velocity 1 m/s.

gorev.tamam: Since 1 · 4 = (1 + 3) · v, v = 1 m/s. The momentum was conserved at 4 kg·m/s and was simply spread over a 4 kg mass.

adimlar.metin: The 1 kg cart A, moving at 4 m/s, hits the 1 kg cart B at rest and sticks. Press play and watch the total kinetic energy at the bottom.

gorev.soru: With B at 1 kg, the kinetic energy dropped from 8 J to 4 J when they stuck. Which statement is true?

secenekler.neden: The total momentum is 4 kg·m/s both before and after. With no external force, momentum is conserved.
Energy is not destroyed, it changes form.

secenekler.yazi: 4 J went into heat and sound
secenekler.neden: The common velocity is 2 m/s, and KE = ½ · 2 · 2² = 4 J. Momentum is conserved, and so is the total energy. Only the kinetic part decreased.

adimlar.metin: A 4 kg rifle will fire a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s.

gorev.soru: At what speed does the rifle recoil?

secenekler.yazi: It does not move at all
secenekler.neden: The rifle pushes the bullet forward and gets an equal push backward (action–reaction).

The bullet goes forward with a momentum of 0.01 · 400 = 4 kg·m/s, and the rifle recoils with 4 kg·m/s. The rifle's speed is 4 / 4 = 1 m/s. The kinetic energies are 800 J and 2 J, so most of the energy goes to the light bullet.
The momenta are equal, not the speeds. The rifle is 400 times heavier than the bullet.

kapanis: Momentum p = m·v is a vector, and its unit is kg·m/s.
Impulse is I = F·Δt = Δp, and it equals the area under the force–time graph. For the same Δp, a longer time means a smaller force.
For an object that bounces back, Δp is twice that of an object that sticks.
With no external force, the total momentum is conserved in both collisions and explosions.
In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved. It decreases most when objects stick together, and it increases in an explosion.

tork-denge.baslik: Torque, equilibrium, and center of mass
tork-denge.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Push the door, balance the seesaw, hang the bar, and tip the box.

adimlar.metin: The turning effect, or torque, is the force times the distance from the hinge. Opening this door takes a torque of 12 N·m. Put your hand where 20 N is enough.

gorev.tamam: At d = 0.6 m, F = 12 / 0.6 = 20 N is enough, and farther out even less will do. If you push 0.2 m from the hinge, you need 60 N.

adimlar.metin: You apply a 20 N force to the end of a wrench, at a distance r = 0.5 m from the nut. Change the angle between the force and the wrench and make the torque as large as possible.

gorev.tamam: At θ = 90°, τ = 20 · 0.5 · 1 = 10 N·m. When the force is perpendicular to the wrench, the lever arm is longest (d = r).

adimlar.baslik: When the line passes through the hinge
adimlar.metin: You apply 20 N to a door 0.8 m from the hinge. But the line of the force passes right through the hinge.

gorev.soru: What is the torque on the door, in N·m?

secenekler.neden: If the force were perpendicular to the door, the torque would be 20 · 0.8 = 16. But what is the lever arm here?
A force whose line passes through the pivot has a lever arm d = 0, so τ = 0. However hard you push, the door does not turn. You only press on the hinge.
20 / 0.8 = 25, but torque comes from the product F·d, not from a division.

adimlar.metin: The 300 N child on the left is 2 m from the pivot. At balance the torques in the two directions are equal. Seat the 400 N child where the seesaw stays balanced.

gorev.tamam: 400 · 1.5 = 600 N·m, which equals 300 · 2. The opposite torques are equal, so Στ = 0. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot. Ignoring the weight of the board, the pivot pushes up with 700 N, so ΣF = 0.

adimlar.metin: A 4 m uniform bar weighing 40 N is supported at both ends, and its weight acts at its middle. Slide the 60 N load and make the force carried by support B 65 N.

kontroller.etiket: Distance of the load from A

gorev.tamam: About A, N<sub>B</sub> · 4 = 40 · 2 + 60 · 3, so N<sub>B</sub> = 65 N. From ΣF = 0, N<sub>A</sub> = 100 − 65 = 35 N. The closer the load is to B, the more B carries.

adimlar.metin: A light bar has 2 kg at its left end and a mass at its right end, 4 m away. You hang the bar from the point at 3 m. Change the mass on the right and make the bar hang level.

gorev.tamam: x<sub>CM</sub> = (2·0 + 6·4) / (2 + 6) = 3 m. A bar hung from its center of mass stays balanced. The center of mass is closer to the heavier part.

adimlar.metin: You put two boxes with the same base on a rough board that tilts slowly. The boxes do not slide.

gorev.soru: Which one tips over first?

secenekler.neden: The low box has a low center of gravity. So its vertical line does not easily leave the base.
Their bases are the same, but their centers of gravity are at different heights.
The tall box has a high center of gravity. At about 22° its vertical line leaves the base and the box tips over. The low box holds out until 45°.

kapanis: Torque is τ = F·d = F·r·sinθ, and its unit is N·m. The lever arm d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force.
A force whose line passes through the pivot has zero torque. The largest torque comes at θ = 90°.
Equilibrium needs both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. The weight of a uniform bar acts at its middle.
The center of mass is x<sub>CM</sub> = Σm·x / Σm, and it is closer to the heavier part.
If the vertical line from the center of gravity falls outside the base, the object tips over. A low center of gravity and a wide base make tipping harder.

madde-ozellikleri.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Weigh, pour, mix, and find the density yourself.

adimlar.metin: One pan of an equal-arm balance holds 1 kg of iron, and the other holds 1 kg of cotton. What happens when you pull out the supports?

gorev.soru: What happens when the pans are released?

secenekler.neden: An equal-arm balance compares masses, and both are 1 kg (ignoring the buoyancy of air). The cotton takes up far more space, but a large volume does not mean a large mass.
Iron seems heavy because it fits in a small space, but the masses are equal.
The cotton takes up more space. But a large volume does not mean a large mass.

adimlar.metin: You pour water into a graduated cylinder, and the scale shows only the mass of the water. Change the volume of the water and make the mass 50 g. Watch the ratio m / V as you do.

gorev.tamam: 50 cm³ of water came to 50 g. When the volume changed, the mass changed in the same proportion, but the ratio m / V stayed at 1 g/cm³. So density does not depend on the amount of a substance.

adimlar.metin: We plotted the mass of three substances against their volume. Each one makes a straight line through the origin.

gorev.soru: Which substance has the highest density?

secenekler.neden: A has the steepest line, so it has the most mass for the same volume. A is aluminum (2.7 g/cm³), B is water (1 g/cm³), and C is wood (about 0.5 g/cm³).
B's line has a medium slope. At the same volume, say 20 cm³, which one has more mass?
C's line is the shallowest. It has the least mass for the same volume, so its density is the lowest.

adimlar.metin: Change the density of the object and leave it suspended in the water.

gorev.tamam: When the (average) density of the object equals that of water, the object stays suspended. If it is lower the object floats, and if it is higher the object sinks. For hollow objects the average density is what counts. That is why a steel ship floats, and you will see the details in the Buoyancy topic.

adimlar.metin: You add alcohol (0.8 g/cm³) to 100 cm³ of water (1 g/cm³). Set the amount of alcohol and make the density of the mixture 0.9 g/cm³.

gorev.tamam: When you mix equal volumes, the result is the average of the two densities. (100 + 80) g ÷ 200 cm³ = 0.9 g/cm³.

adimlar.metin: Water adheres to glass more strongly than it holds on to its own particles. You dip three glass tubes into water.

gorev.soru: In which tube does the water rise highest?

secenekler.neden: Water climbs by adhering to the glass, and the thinner the tube, the higher it rises. This is called capillary action. It is why water rises in plants and why a paper towel gets wet. Mercury, which does not adhere to glass, drops lower in a thin tube.
In a wide tube the water to be pulled up is much heavier. Adhesion cannot hold it up.
The height depends on how thin the tube is.

kapanis: Mass and volume are common properties found in all matter. Density is a distinguishing property that identifies a substance.
Density is ρ = m / V. On a mass–volume graph the slope of the line gives the density, and a steeper line means a denser substance.
An object whose average density is lower than water's floats, one with equal density stays suspended, and one with higher density sinks.
The density of a mixture is ρ = m<sub>total</sub> / V<sub>final</sub>. The result lies between the two densities.
The difference between adhesion and cohesion leads to capillary action. Water rises higher in a thinner tube.

basinc.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Drop the brick, step on the snow, lower the diver, and lift the car.

adimlar.metin: Two bricks are identical, and each weighs 20 N. One stands upright and will touch the sponge with its small face. The other lies flat and will touch it with its wide face.

gorev.soru: When released, which one sinks deeper into the sponge?

secenekler.neden: The flat brick touches a wider area. Its weight is spread over a large area.
The force is the same, but the upright brick puts it on an area 4 times smaller. A smaller area means a larger pressure. The upright brick exerts 4000 Pa, and the flat one 1000 Pa.
The weights are equal, but the areas they touch are different.

adimlar.baslik: Do not sink into the snow
adimlar.metin: You weigh 600 N and you are standing on snow. This snow can hold a pressure of at most 3000 Pa. Make the area of your shoes larger and do not sink in.

gorev.tamam: 600 N ÷ 0.2 m² = 3000 Pa. Snowshoes do not change your weight. They spread it over a large area.

adimlar.metin: The density of water is 1000 kg/m³, and g is about 10 m/s². Lower the diver and watch the pressure. Stop at the depth where the water pressure is 200 000 Pa.

gorev.tamam: 1000 × 10 × 20 = 200 000 Pa. When the depth doubled, the liquid pressure doubled too.

adimlar.metin: We will fill a wide, a narrow, and a funnel-shaped container with water to a height of 20 cm. The funnel holds the most water, and the narrow one the least.

gorev.soru: In which one is the liquid pressure at the bottom the largest?

secenekler.neden: The funnel holds the most water, but the formula is P = ρ·g·h, and the amount is not in it.
A wide base makes the total force larger, but the force on each unit of area stays the same.
Liquid pressure depends only on depth and density, and 1000 × 10 × 0.2 = 2000 Pa. The shape of the container and the amount of water make no difference. This is called the hydrostatic paradox.

adimlar.metin: The small piston has an area of 10 cm², and you apply 200 N to it. Find the smallest large piston that can hold up the 10 000 N car.

gorev.tamam: The large piston must have an area of 500 cm², 50 times the small one. 200 N × 50 = 10 000 N. But you lose in distance. If you push the small piston 50 cm, the car rises only 1 cm.

adimlar.metin: At sea level water boils at 100 °C. Go up and find the altitude where water boils at 80 °C.

gorev.tamam: At about 6000 m the outside pressure drops so much that water boils at 80 °C. That is why food takes longer to cook on high mountains.

kapanis: Pressure is the size of the force acting perpendicular to a unit of surface, P = F / A. It is a scalar, and its unit is the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).
For the same force, a smaller area means a larger pressure. That is why a knife cuts and why snowshoes keep you from sinking.
Liquid pressure is P = ρ·g·h. It grows with depth and does not depend on the shape of the container or the amount of liquid.
By Pascal's principle, pressure in an enclosed liquid is transmitted everywhere. In a hydraulic system F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
Atmospheric pressure is 76 cmHg (1 atm) at sea level. It drops as you go higher, and water boils at a lower temperature.

kaldirma-kuvveti.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Lower the stone into water, load the ship, and lift the balloon.

adimlar.metin: A 10 cm cube is under water. The water presses on it from every direction. The forces on the sides cancel each other. Look at the top and bottom faces.

gorev.soru: Which face has the larger force on it?

secenekler.neden: The top face is closer to the surface of the water. Does pressure increase or decrease with depth?
The bottom face is deeper, and liquid pressure increases with depth. The push from below is 10 N larger than the push from above. This difference is the upward buoyant force (Fb).
The sides are equal because they are at the same depth. The top and bottom faces are at different depths.

adimlar.metin: A stone hanging from a spring scale reads 5 N in air, and its volume is 200 cm³. Slowly lower the stone into the water until it is fully submerged. Then look at the reading.

gorev.tamam: The reading dropped to 3 N. So F<sub>b</sub> = 5 − 3 = 2 N. Let us check: V<sub>sub</sub>·ρ<sub>liq</sub>·g = 0.0002 m³ × 1000 kg/m³ × 10 m/s² = 2 N.

adimlar.metin: The 10 cm cube from before is fully under water. Move it up and down. How do the forces on the top and bottom faces change?

gorev.soru: What happens to the buoyant force when you lower the fully submerged cube deeper?

secenekler.neden: It is true that the pressures increase. But both increase together. Look at the difference.
Going deeper does not reduce the force on any face. Look at the difference.
The forces on both faces increase by the same amount, and the difference stays at 10 N. F<sub>b</sub> depends on the submerged volume, not on the depth.

adimlar.metin: You put a 1000 cm³ (6 N) wooden cube with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ into different liquids. Change the density of the liquid so that the cube floats exactly half submerged.

gorev.tamam: Since 0.6 / 1.2 = 1/2, half of the cube is submerged. In every liquid where the cube floats, F<sub>b</sub> = W = 6 N. Only the submerged volume changes, and the object sinks less in a denser liquid.

adimlar.metin: Load containers onto the ship. Stop when the water reaches the load line on the hull (yellow circle).

gorev.tamam: Each container made the ship sit a little deeper. To balance the extra weight, the ship must displace more water. The load line shows how deep the ship can safely sit.

adimlar.metin: The volume of a submarine does not change, and when it is fully submerged F<sub>b</sub> is constant too. The submarine has taken seawater into its ballast tanks.

gorev.soru: What does a submarine do after taking water into its tanks?

secenekler.neden: The water entering the tanks makes the submarine heavier.

A submarine changes its weight, not its volume. With water taken in, W > F<sub>b</sub> and the submarine dives. When the water is blown out with compressed air, W < F<sub>b</sub> and it rises. If W = F<sub>b</sub>, it stays suspended.
The volume, and so F<sub>b</sub>, stayed the same, but the weight increased.

adimlar.metin: 1 m³ of helium gets a buoyant force of about 12 N from the air, and its own weight is about 1.7 N. The basket and the balloon skin weigh 40 N. Make the balloon larger and lift it off the ground.

gorev.tamam: At 4 m³, F<sub>b</sub> = 48 N, and the total weight is 40 + 6.8 = 46.8 N. So the balloon rises. Each m³ of helium gives a net lift of about 10 N.

kapanis: The buoyant force comes from a pressure difference. The bottom face is deeper, so it is pushed harder.
By Archimedes' principle, Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g. The apparent weight equals W − Fb.
Lowering a fully submerged object deeper does not change F<sub>b</sub>.
For floating and suspended objects F<sub>b</sub> = W. For a floating object V<sub>sub</sub> / V = ρ<sub>obj</sub> / ρ<sub>liq</sub>.
A ship floats by displacing a lot of water, a submarine dives by changing its weight, and a balloon flies on the buoyant force of the air.

isi-sicaklik.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Set the thermometer, heat water and iron, melt ice and expand a rail.

adimlar.metin: At 1 atm, a boiling drop of water and a boiling bucket of water are both at 100 °C. Internal energy is the sum of the energies of all the particles.

gorev.soru: Which one has the larger internal energy?

secenekler.neden: The temperatures are equal, so the average energy is equal. But internal energy is a total, not an average.
The average energy is the same, but the bucket has far more particles. Internal energy is a total, so it depends on the amount of matter. Temperature does not.
The drop has very few particles. Total energy grows with the number of particles.

adimlar.metin: On the Kelvin scale, you find the temperature by adding 273 to the Celsius value. Set the thermometer to 300 K.

gorev.tamam: 300 − 273 = 27 °C. On the Fahrenheit scale this is 1.8 × 27 + 32 = 80.6 °F.

adimlar.metin: 100 g of water and 100 g of iron are placed on identical heaters. Each will absorb the same amount of heat, 1000 cal. Both start at 20 °C.

gorev.soru: Which one's temperature rises more?

secenekler.neden: Water has a very large specific heat. So the same heat warms it only a little.
The masses and the heat are equal, but the substances are different.
Heating 1 g of iron by 1 °C takes about 0.11 cal, while 1 g of water takes 1 cal. The same 1000 cal warms the water by 10 °C and the iron by about 91 °C.

adimlar.metin: 200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with cold water at 20 °C. Find the amount of cold water that brings the mixture to 44 °C.

gorev.tamam: 200·(80 − 44) = 7200 cal was given off, and 300·(44 − 20) = 7200 cal was absorbed. There is more cold water, so the equilibrium is closer to 20 °C.

adimlar.metin: There is 10 g of ice at 0 °C, and the heat of fusion of ice is L = 80 cal/g. Melt all the ice, but do not warm the water.

gorev.tamam: It takes 10 g × 80 cal/g = 800 cal. The temperature stayed at 0 °C throughout the melting. Any heat supplied after this warms the water.

adimlar.metin: There is a 6 mm gap between 10 m steel rails, and for steel λ is about 1.2·10⁻⁵ 1/°C. Raise the temperature and find the moment the gap just closes.

gorev.tamam: 10 000 mm × 1.2·10⁻⁵ × 50 = 6 mm. On a hotter day the gap is not enough and the rails buckle. That is why gaps are left between rails and expansion joints are built into bridges.

kapanis: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, and it does not depend on the amount of matter. Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold.
The Kelvin value is T = t + 273, and the Fahrenheit value is F = 1.8·t + 32.
When there is no change of state, the heat absorbed is Q = m·c·ΔT, and a substance with a large specific heat warms slowly. At thermal equilibrium, heat gained equals heat lost.
During a change of state, the heat absorbed is Q = m·L, and the temperature stays constant.
A heated solid gets longer, and the change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT.

basit-harmonik-hareket.ozet: Pull the spring and see the restoring force. Watch the oscillation, read the position-time graph and set the period. Take a pendulum to the Moon, find how the energy is shared, and catch resonance with a swing.

adimlar.metin: A spring pulls an object that is a distance x from equilibrium back with a force F = −k · x. Here k = 50 N/m. Move the object to a place where the spring pulls it to the left with 5 N.

gorev.tamam: For x = +0.1 m, F = −50 · 0.1 = −5 N. The object is to the right of equilibrium, and the force points left. The spring always pulls the object toward equilibrium.
gorev.ipucu: For the force to point left, the object must be to the right of equilibrium. 5 / 50 = 0.1 m.

adimlar.baslik: What happens when you let go?
adimlar.metin: You pull the object 10 cm and let go, and there is no friction. The red arrow will show the acceleration and the green arrow the velocity.

gorev.soru: How does the object move?

secenekler.neden: At equilibrium the force is zero, but the object is at its fastest at that moment. So its speed carries it past equilibrium.

secenekler.yazi: It goes a little past equilibrium and stops
secenekler.neden: That is damped oscillation. In damped oscillation friction turns the energy into heat, but here there is no friction.

secenekler.yazi: It goes back and forth between two ends
secenekler.neden: At equilibrium the speed is greatest and the acceleration is zero. At the ends it is the other way around. There is no friction, so the amplitude stays 10 cm.

adimlar.metin: An object on a vertical spring was released from +A at t = 0. The period is T = 2 s, and the graph is the curve x = A·cos(ωt). Slide the time and find the moment the object first reaches −A.

gorev.tamam: The object reaches −A at T/2 = 1 s. It passes equilibrium at T/4 = 0.5 s and is back at the start at T = 2 s.
gorev.ipucu: One full back-and-forth trip takes T. Reaching −A takes half of that.

adimlar.metin: The object oscillates on the end of the spring without friction, and the position-time graph runs below it. When you change the spring constant, the mass and the amplitude, the oscillation changes right away. Find the following for yourself.

bulgular.yazi: With k = 40 N/m and 1 kg, set the amplitude to 10, then to 20 cm. Does the period change?
bulgular.tamam: The period stays 0.99 s. When the amplitude doubles, the object travels twice as far but also twice as fast. So the period does not depend on the amplitude.

bulgular.yazi: Find a way to double the period (≈ 2 s).
bulgular.tamam: The relation T = 2π√(m/k) contains a square root. So to double the period you must make the mass 4 times larger or cut k to one quarter.

bulgular.yazi: Now bring the period down to 0.5 s.
bulgular.tamam: You need a light mass and a stiff spring. For m = 0.5 kg and k = 80 N/m, T = 2π√(0.5/80) ≈ 0.5 s. A stiffer spring gives a larger restoring force, and the oscillation speeds up.

adimlar.metin: This pendulum swings through small angles. Change the length of the string and the mass of the ball, and play it at least twice.

gorev.soru: What does the period of the pendulum depend on?

secenekler.neden: The period comes out the same with the heavy ball and the light one.
In the trial where you change only the mass, the period does not change.
The period grows with the square root of the string length. When the string is 4 times longer, the period doubles. The mass does not change the period.

adimlar.metin: The same 1 m pendulum will swing on Earth and on the Moon. On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s², one sixth of its value on Earth.

gorev.soru: What is the period of the pendulum on the Moon?

secenekler.neden: The period of a pendulum depends on g: T = 2π√(L/g).
The period is inversely proportional to √g, not to g.
When g drops to one sixth, the period becomes √6 ≈ 2.45 times longer. So the period is about 4.9 s instead of 2 s. That is why a pendulum clock runs slow on the Moon.

adimlar.metin: The potential energy is ½ · k · x², and the total energy is ½ · k · A². The spring constant is k = 50 N/m and the amplitude is A = 10 cm. Move the object to a place where 75% of the energy is kinetic.

gorev.tamam: At x = A/2 = 5 cm, E<sub>p</sub> = ½ · 50 · 0.05² = 0.0625 J. This is one quarter of the total energy (0.25 J). The other 75% is kinetic. The speed here is about 87% of the maximum speed.
gorev.ipucu: The share of potential energy must be 25%: x²/A² = 1/4.

adimlar.metin: Push the swing at regular intervals, always in the same direction. Find the push interval that makes the swing grow the most.

gorev.tamam: The swing's own period is 2 s, so its natural frequency is 0.5 Hz. Every push came while the swing was moving the same way, and the amplitude grew. This is called resonance. The frequency of the outside push must equal the natural frequency. Friction limits the amplitude.
gorev.ipucu: The pushes should line up with one full back-and-forth trip of the swing.

kapanis: The restoring force F = −k·x always points toward equilibrium.
The speed is greatest at equilibrium (ωA). The acceleration is greatest at the ends (ω²A).
For a mass on a spring T = 2π√(m/k), and for a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g). The period does not depend on the amplitude.
The period of a pendulum does not depend on the mass, and it gets longer when g gets smaller. The period of a mass on a spring does not depend on g.
The total energy is E = ½kA², and it is constant. At an end all the energy is potential, and at equilibrium it is all kinetic.

dalgalar.ozet: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves, set the wavelength with v = λ·f, send a wave into another medium, see what amplitude does, reflect a pulse and make waves interfere.

adimlar.metin: Send a wave first along a rope, then along a spring, and watch the red particles.

gorev.soru: Does the red particle travel along with the wave?

secenekler.neden: Look at the dashed line. The particle stays around the place where it started.
A wave carries energy, not matter. When you throw a stone into water the rings move outward, but a floating leaf just bobs up and down in place.
In a longitudinal wave too, the particle moves back and forth and returns to the same place.

adimlar.metin: The speed of a wave is v = λ · f. The wave will now pass from a thin rope to a thick rope.

gorev.soru: What changes on the thick rope?

secenekler.yazi: Speed and λ decrease, f is the same
secenekler.neden: The wave slows down on the thick rope. The frequency does not change, so by v = λ·f the wavelength gets shorter too.

secenekler.yazi: f decreases, λ is the same
secenekler.neden: The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change.
On the thick rope the waves bunch up and the front slows down.

adimlar.metin: Amplitude is the height from equilibrium to a crest. The two ropes are identical. The upper wave has amplitude A, and the lower one 3A.

gorev.soru: Which wave gets ahead?

secenekler.neden: A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy, but it does not travel faster.
A small amplitude does not speed a wave up. Both waves are in the same medium.
The two waves travel at the same speed on identical ropes. The medium sets the speed, not the amplitude.

adimlar.metin: The source shakes the rope, and the wave travels to the right. The triangle follows a crest, and the red dot is a piece of the rope. Change the frequency, the wave speed (the tension in the rope) and the amplitude. Find the following for yourself.

bulgular.yazi: With the speed at 4 m/s, raise the frequency from 1 Hz to 2 Hz. What happens to the wavelength?
bulgular.tamam: λ dropped from 4 m to 2 m. On the same rope the speed does not change. So when the frequency doubles, the wavelength is cut in half: v = λ·f.

bulgular.yazi: Set the frequency to 4 Hz but keep the wavelength at 2 m.
bulgular.tamam: For the wavelength to stay the same, the speed had to double as well, so you tightened the rope. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency.

bulgular.yazi: Bring the wavelength down to 0.5 m and watch the red dot.
bulgular.tamam: At a speed of 2 m/s and a frequency of 4 Hz, λ = 0.5 m. While the wave traveled to the right, the red dot only vibrated up and down. So a wave carries energy, not matter.

adimlar.metin: A single disturbance on a spring is called a pulse. Send the pulse first to a fixed end tied to a wall, then to a free end with a ring sliding on a rod.

gorev.soru: At which end does the pulse come back inverted?

secenekler.neden: At the free end the ring rises with the pulse, and the pulse comes back as a crest.
The pulse pulls the wall up, and the wall pulls the rope down. This is an action-reaction pair. So the crest comes back as a trough.
In the trial with the free end, the pulse came back as a crest.

adimlar.metin: Two pulses are heading toward each other. When they meet at the same point, their displacements add. Make the rope look flat at the moment they meet.

gorev.tamam: When a crest met an equal trough, the displacements canceled each other. This is called destructive interference.
gorev.ipucu: To cancel a crest you need an equal trough.

kapanis: A wave carries energy, not matter. The particles of the medium vibrate in place.
In a transverse wave the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel, and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Sound is a longitudinal wave.
The speed of a wave is v = λ·f. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency. Amplitude changes the energy, not the speed.
A pulse reflects inverted from a fixed end and upright from a free end. When waves meet, their displacements add.
Pushes at the natural frequency make the amplitude grow. This is called resonance.

deprem.ozet: Release the stress built up on a fault and race the P and S waves to a station. Turn magnitude into energy, and drive buildings into resonance on a shake table.

adimlar.metin: The two sides of the fault are slowly pushed in opposite directions, but friction keeps the fault locked. Press play and watch the road.

gorev.soru: What happened to the road when the stress exceeded the strength?

secenekler.yazi: It splits in two, and the pieces stay straight but offset
secenekler.neden: The rock slips suddenly and the bend straightens out, but the two sides are now offset. The stored energy spreads out as waves.
The bend in the road is a sign of stress. When the fault breaks, the stress is released and the road straightens.

secenekler.yazi: It returns to its old straight shape, with no offset
secenekler.neden: The blocks really did move during this time. The break completes that slip all at once.

adimlar.metin: Two kinds of waves, P and S, leave the focus at the same moment. The station is 120 km away.

gorev.soru: Which one reaches the station first?

secenekler.neden: P travels at about 6 km/s and S at about 3.5 km/s. Over 120 km, P arrives in 20 s and S in about 34 s.
S shakes harder, but it is slower.
The two waves leave at the same moment, but their speeds are different. So S falls behind.

adimlar.metin: Each second of difference between P and S means about 8 km of distance. Place the station where there will be 10 seconds between P and S. Then press play.

gorev.tamam: The distance is about 84 km. The P wave arrives in 14 seconds and the S wave in 24 seconds. Each second of difference is about 8.4 km. That is why the rule is d ≈ 8 km × Δt.
gorev.ipucu: Each 1 second of difference means about 8 km of distance.

adimlar.metin: When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times. Raise the magnitude. The square stands for the energy released.

gorev.tamam: A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 1000 times (32 × 32) the energy of a magnitude 5. A small difference in magnitude is a huge difference in energy.
gorev.ipucu: Each +1 in magnitude means about 32 times the energy. 32 × 32 is about 1000.

adimlar.metin: Every building has its own period of oscillation. The table will shake slowly, with a period of 2 s (0.5 Hz). The natural periods of the buildings are written below them.

gorev.soru: Which building sways the most?

secenekler.neden: The period of this building is about 0.3 s. In slow shaking it moves along with the ground and does not bend.
The period of this building is about 1 s, which does not match the 2 s shaking.
The period of this building is about 2 s, equal to that of the shaking. So it goes into resonance. Long-period shaking is dangerous for tall buildings.

adimlar.metin: A building goes into resonance when the frequency of the shaking equals its own frequency (f = 1/T). Set the frequency, bring the 3-story building into resonance, and press play.

gorev.tamam: The period of the 3-story building is ≈ 0.3 s, so f ≈ 3.3 Hz. Short-period shaking on hard ground puts stress on low buildings.
gorev.ipucu: f = 1 / T. The period of the 3-story building is T ≈ 0.1 × 3 = 0.3 s.

adimlar.metin: The building and the shaking are the same. Play it first without the isolator, then turn the isolator on.

gorev.soru: How does an isolator protect the building?

secenekler.yazi: It lengthens the building's period, so less shaking gets through
secenekler.neden: The flexible bearings absorb the motion of the ground. The building's period moves far from that of the shaking, and resonance is avoided.

secenekler.yazi: It makes the building stiffer and heavier
secenekler.neden: Stiffness shortens the period. An isolator does the opposite and makes the building flexible at its base.
The wave still arrives, and the ground shakes the same way. What changes is how much of the shaking is passed on to the building.

kapanis: An earthquake is the sudden release of stress built up on a locked fault.
Each second between P and S means about 8 km of distance.
When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times.
If the period of the shaking is close to the building's natural period, there is resonance. An isolator prevents this.

elektrostatik.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Rub the glass, touch the spheres together, charge by grounding and set the Coulomb force.

adimlar.metin: Charge does not appear from nothing. Only electrons pass from one object to the other. Rub the glass rod with the silk cloth.

gorev.soru: What charge does the glass rod have after rubbing?

secenekler.neden: The one that is (−) is the silk, which gains the electrons.
The glass gives electrons to the silk. The glass, now short of electrons, becomes (+), and the silk becomes (−) by the same amount. Total charge is conserved.
Two electrons moved to the silk. The glass is no longer neutral.

adimlar.metin: Spheres that touch share charge in proportion to their radii. Sphere A has 12 μC and B is neutral. Choose the radius of B so that B ends up with 8 μC after they touch.

gorev.tamam: When the radii are 1 : 2, the 12 μC divides as 4 : 8. The total charge is still 12 μC. In contact, charge is conserved and both spheres get the same sign.
gorev.ipucu: B must take 2/3 of the total.

adimlar.metin: A (−) charged rod approaches a neutral conducting sphere without touching it. The electrons in the sphere can move freely.

gorev.soru: What happens to the side of the sphere near the rod?

secenekler.neden: Electrons are repelled by the (−) rod and escape to the far side.
The total charge is zero, but the charges shift.
Electrons are repelled and move to the far side. The near side becomes (+) and the far side (−). The sphere as a whole is still neutral. This is called polarization.

adimlar.metin: Now the order is: bring the rod near, connect the sphere to the ground, cut the connection, and remove the rod. Watch this sequence.

gorev.soru: What charge is the sphere left with?

secenekler.neden: The repelled electrons escape to the ground, and they cannot come back because the connection is cut first. The sphere is left with the sign opposite to the rod.
An object charged by induction takes the sign opposite to the rod. Electrons left the sphere.
Charge can move without contact too. Here the electrons flowed to the ground.

adimlar.metin: A (+) rod has been brought near the knob of an electroscope. By induction the leaves get the same sign and repel each other. Move the rod away.

gorev.soru: What happens to the leaves when the rod moves away?

secenekler.neden: The induction weakens, and the charge on the leaves decreases.
No charge passed to the electroscope. When the induction ends, the leaves go back to how they were.
There was no contact, so the total charge of the electroscope is zero. When the rod moves away, the charges return to their places and the leaves close.

adimlar.metin: The force between two charges is F = k·q₁·q₂ / r². q₁ = +4 μC. Set q₂ and the distance so that the force is an attraction of 0.1 N (k ≈ 9·10⁹ N·m²/C²).

gorev.tamam: For q₂ = −1 μC and r = 60 cm, F = 9·10⁹ · 4·10⁻⁶ · 1·10⁻⁶ / 0.36 = 0.1 N. Opposite charges attract, and like charges repel.
gorev.ipucu: For attraction q₂ must be (−). At 30 cm, −1 μC gives 0.4 N. Double the distance.

adimlar.metin: Electric field lines show the direction a (+) test charge placed there would be pushed. Change the sign of the charge on the right.

gorev.soru: Where do field lines start and where do they end?

secenekler.neden: The lines point out of a (+) charge and into a (−) charge, and they never cross.
The direction of the field is the direction a (+) test charge would be pushed. That direction points away from a (+) charge.

secenekler.yazi: They exist only between the two charges
secenekler.neden: The lines spread in every direction. For two charges of the same sign, an empty region is left between them.

kapanis: Charge is quantized (e = 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C) and conserved. In charging, only electrons are transferred.
With friction, glass becomes (+) and silk (−). With contact, charge is shared in proportion to the radii and with the same sign.
An object charged by induction and grounding gets the sign opposite to the rod. For this, the connection must be cut before the rod is removed.
By Coulomb's law F = k·q₁·q₂ / r². Opposite charges attract and like charges repel.
Field lines leave (+), enter (−), and never cross.

elektrik-akimi.ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Close the switch, lengthen the wire, connect bulbs in series and in parallel, and solve a mixed circuit.

adimlar.metin: Electrons leave from the (−) terminal, and conventional current runs the opposite way. Close the switch.

gorev.tamam: The circuit is complete. If 30 C of charge passes through the cross-section in 1 minute, the current is I = 30 / 60 = 0.5 A. No current forms in an open circuit.

adimlar.metin: The resistance is 4 Ω. Increase the voltage and get a current of 2 A. Use the relation V = I · R for this.

gorev.tamam: V = I · R = 2 · 4 = 8 V. If the voltage doubles, the current doubles too. That is why the V–I graph is a straight line.
gorev.ipucu: Since I = V / R, to get 2 A you need V = 2 · 4.

adimlar.metin: On a V–I graph (V vertical, I horizontal), the line's slope gives the resistance.

gorev.soru: Which one has the larger resistance?

secenekler.neden: Y is flatter. It needs less voltage for the same current, so its resistance is small.
The slopes are different. The lines of conductors with equal resistance would lie on top of each other.
X is steeper. It needs more voltage for the same current, so its R = V / I value is large. When they are connected in parallel, Y carries more of the current.

adimlar.metin: The resistance of a wire increases with length and decreases with cross-section. The wire is twice as long. Adjust the cross-section so that the resistance is R₀ again.

gorev.tamam: The length doubled, and so did the cross-section. So R = 2/2 · R₀ = R₀. This is why a long extension cord is made thicker.
gorev.ipucu: The ratio L / A must be 1.

adimlar.metin: First connect the bulbs in parallel, then unscrew one bulb. Try the same with the series connection.

gorev.soru: When one bulb is unscrewed, in which connection does the other keep glowing?

secenekler.neden: A series connection has a single path. When one bulb is unscrewed, the circuit opens and they all go out.
