In a parallel connection, each bulb has its own branch. Even if one is unscrewed, the other still gets the same 12 V (with an ideal battery) and glows just as brightly. That is why home wiring is parallel.
In a parallel connection, the path of the other branch stays open to current. You can also see in the scene that the other bulb stays on when you unscrew one.

adimlar.metin: The internal resistance of an ammeter is almost zero. You connected it in parallel with the lamp by mistake.

gorev.soru: What happens if an ammeter is connected in parallel with a lamp?

secenekler.neden: The current skips the lamp. It passes through the ammeter, which has almost no resistance.
A path with an internal resistance of about zero has opened. The current chooses this path.

secenekler.yazi: The lamp goes out, a large current flows
secenekler.neden: The internal resistance of an ammeter is almost zero. So a short circuit path opens across the lamp. The lamp goes out, a very large current is drawn from the battery, and the ammeter can burn out.

adimlar.metin: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors connected in parallel. Adjust the battery so that 3 A flows in the main branch.

gorev.tamam: The resistance of the parallel part is 6·3/(6+3) = 2 Ω, and the equivalent resistance is 6 Ω. So V = 3 · 6 = 18 V. 6 V drops across the parallel part. 1 A passes through the 6 Ω and 2 A through the 3 Ω, and the total is 3 A again. This is the junction rule.
gorev.ipucu: First reduce the parallel part to a single resistor: 6·3/(6+3).

kapanis: Current is the charge that passes per unit time and is found with I = q / t. Conventional current is opposite to the electrons.
According to Ohm's law, V = I · R. The slope of the V–I graph gives the resistance.
The resistance of a wire is found with R = ρ · L / A. A wire drawn out to twice its length has 4 times the resistance.
In series the current is shared and Req is the sum. In parallel the voltage is shared and Req is smaller than the smallest resistor.
An ammeter is connected in series (internal resistance ≈ 0), and a voltmeter in parallel (internal resistance very large).

elektriksel-enerji.ozet: Charge the phone and compare the brightness of the bulbs. Heat the wire, read the label, and lower the bill. Switch to LED without blowing the fuse.

adimlar.metin: The energy transferred is found with W = V · I · t. The charger delivers 5 V and 2 A. Transfer 36 000 J of energy to the phone.

gorev.tamam: W = 5 · 2 · 3600 = 36 000 J. 1 hour is 3600 seconds. Do not forget to convert minutes to seconds.
gorev.ipucu: How many minutes is 36 000 / (5 · 2) seconds?

adimlar.metin: The brightness of a bulb is set by its power. The resistances of the bulbs are 2 Ω and 4 Ω. In series the current is shared, so P = I² · R is used. In parallel the voltage is shared, so P = V² / R is used. Try both connections.

gorev.soru: Which bulb is brighter when they are in series?

secenekler.neden: In series the current is shared, and since P = I² · R, the smaller resistor uses less power. The 2 Ω bulb glows brighter only in parallel.
In series the same current passes through both, and since P = I² · R, the larger resistor uses more power. In parallel, P = V² / R, so the 2 Ω bulb glows brighter.
The resistances are different. So they use different powers at the same current.

adimlar.metin: Heat is found with Q = I² · R · t. A 10 Ω wire gives 600 J of heat in 1 minute at a current of 1 A. Make the heat 4 times as large.

gorev.tamam: When the current doubles, the heat becomes 2² = 4 times as large: 2² · 10 · 60 = 2400 J. That is why fuses and cable thickness matter.
gorev.ipucu: Heat increases with the square of the current.

adimlar.metin: The heater's label says 220 V, 2000 W. Its resistance is R = V² / P = 24.2 Ω and does not change. We plug the heater into a 110 V outlet.

gorev.soru: How many watts does the heater use at 110 V?

secenekler.neden: The voltage was halved, but power is proportional to V². The square of one half is one quarter.
The power on the label is valid only at 220 V.
The resistance is constant, so P = V² / R = 110² / 24.2 = 500 W. When the voltage is halved, the power drops to one quarter.

adimlar.metin: Energy (kWh) is power (kW) multiplied by time (hours). A 1.5 kW air conditioner runs for 30 days, and 1 kWh costs 3 TL. Adjust the daily use so that the monthly cost does not exceed 270 TL.

gorev.tamam: If it runs 2 hours a day, it uses 1.5 · 2 · 30 = 90 kWh, and the cost is 90 · 3 = 270 TL. Halving the time also halves the bill.
gorev.ipucu: 270 TL / 3 TL makes 90 kWh. How many hours is 90 / (1.5 · 30)?

adimlar.metin: The fuse is rated 16 A, and the 2000 W heater is on. Switch on one more device next to it, but do not blow the fuse.

gorev.tamam: 9.1 A + 5 A makes about 14.1 A, and this value is below the limit. With the kettle the total would be 19.1 A, and the fuse would blow. A fuse protects the cable from overheating.
gorev.ipucu: The current of each device is found with I = P / 220. The total current must not exceed 16 A.

adimlar.metin: A 60 W incandescent bulb and a 9 W LED give the same light. Switch to LED.

gorev.soru: If it is on 5 hours a day, how much energy does the LED save in a year?

secenekler.neden: That only looks at the 9 W the LED uses. The difference is 60 − 9 = 51 W.
51 is the difference in watts. It has to be multiplied by the number of hours and days.
The difference is 51 W. 51 W · 5 hours · 365 days makes about 93 000 Wh, that is 93 kWh.

kapanis: Electrical energy is found with W = V · I · t. Power is P = V · I = I² · R = V² / R.
Power sets the brightness. In series the larger resistor glows brighter, and in parallel the smaller one does.
Heat is found with Q = I² · R · t. When the current doubles, the heat becomes four times as large.
The kWh is a unit of energy. The bill is power multiplied by time and by the unit price.
Home wiring is parallel, and the fuse limits the total current. An LED gives the same light with much less energy.

manyetizma.ozet: Push and pull magnets, then break one. Explore the field with a compass and look around a current-carrying wire. Build an electromagnet and measure the force on a wire.

adimlar.metin: Every magnet has an N (north) and an S (south) pole. Right now two N poles face each other. Flip the magnet on the right.

gorev.tamam: Opposite poles attract each other, and like poles repel. Repulsion proves that an object is a magnet. Attraction is not proof, because a magnet also attracts an iron nail.

adimlar.metin: The left half of the bar magnet is the S pole and the right half is the N pole. What happens if you break it right in the middle?

gorev.soru: What happens to the pieces when a magnet is broken in the middle?

secenekler.yazi: One is only N, the other only S
secenekler.neden: Poles cannot be separated from each other. A new pole forms at the broken end of each piece.
Magnetism comes from tiny magnets at the atomic scale. Breaking the magnet does not destroy them.
New poles form at the broken ends right away. The right end of the left piece becomes N, and the left end of the right piece becomes S.

adimlar.metin: Move the compass to the numbered spots and watch how the needle turns.

gorev.soru: Where is the magnetic field strongest?

secenekler.neden: The lines gather and get denser at the poles. The field (B) is strongest there.
The lines are sparse in the middle region. So at spot 2 the field is only of medium strength.
Sparse lines mean a weak field. The field is weak at spots 1 and 6.

adimlar.metin: This is Oersted's experiment, and the wire is perpendicular to the screen. In the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field. Turn on the current, reverse its direction, and look at the compasses.

gorev.soru: If the current goes into the screen (⊗), which way do the field lines circle?

secenekler.neden: That happens when the current flows toward you (⊙). When the current reverses, the field reverses too.
By the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current (into the screen). The curled fingers then turn clockwise.
The field lines of a wire are circles around the wire. The compasses sit tangent to these circles.

adimlar.metin: A current of 2 A flows through the coil. Build an electromagnet that picks up exactly 8 paper clips.

gorev.tamam: 40 turns with an iron core picked up 8 paper clips. The core itself becomes magnetized in the field of the coil and adds to the field.
gorev.ipucu: A coil without a core is weak. First insert the iron core, then adjust the number of turns.

adimlar.metin: A force of F = B·I·L·sinθ acts on a current-carrying wire in a field. Here B = 0.2 T, I = 5 A, and L = 0.5 m. Adjust the angle so that the force is 0.25 N.

gorev.tamam: F = 0.2 · 5 · 0.5 · sin30° = 0.5 · 0.5 = 0.25 N. The force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field (0.5 N). When the wire is parallel to the field, the force is zero.
gorev.ipucu: 0.2 · 5 · 0.5 makes 0.5 N. So sinθ must be 0.5.

adimlar.metin: The commutator is the part that reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn. This motor has no commutator, and the current always flows in the same direction.

gorev.soru: What would the coil do without a commutator?

secenekler.neden: When the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field, the forces on the sides lie along the same line and the torque is zero. The coil swings back and forth around this position.
Once the plane of the loop passes the position perpendicular to the field, the forces pull the coil back. For continuous rotation, the direction of the current has to be reversed.
At the start the forces create a torque and the coil begins to turn. But the coil cannot turn continuously.

kapanis: Like poles repel each other, and opposite poles attract. Repulsion proves that an object is a magnet. There is no magnet with a single pole.
Field lines run from N to S outside the magnet. Where the lines are dense, the field is strong. The N end of a compass shows the direction of the field.
A wire carrying current creates a field around itself: B = 2k·I/d. The direction of the field is found with the right-hand rule.
An electromagnet gets stronger with turns, current, and an iron core.
A force of F = B·I·L·sinθ acts on a wire in a field. Thanks to the commutator, a motor turns this force into continuous rotation.

induksiyon-ac.ozet: Push a magnet into a coil and see Lenz's rule. Slide a rod on rails and spin a generator. Read the grid voltage, adjust a transformer, and cut the transmission loss.

adimlar.metin: When the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a current forms in the coil. This is called electromagnetic induction. Push the magnet into the coil at different speeds and watch the galvanometer.

gorev.soru: What does the galvanometer's deflection depend on?

secenekler.neden: When the magnet stops, the flux does not change and the needle returns to zero.
As the magnet speeds up, the flux through the coil changes in a shorter time. The faster the flux changes, the larger the voltage.
Look at the faded traces of your trials. As the speed increases, the deflection increases too.

adimlar.metin: The N pole of the magnet is approaching the coil quickly. The current that forms in the coil also turns the coil into a magnet.

gorev.soru: What does the face of the coil toward the magnet become?

secenekler.neden: If that were so, the magnet would speed up on its own, and energy would be produced from nothing.
The current through the coil forces the coil to behave like a magnet.
The coil repels the approaching N pole and so opposes its approach. The work you do pushing the magnet against this repulsion turns into electrical energy.

adimlar.metin: For a sliding rod, ε = B · L · v. B = 0.5 T, and the length of the rod is L = 0.4 m. Adjust the speed so that the voltage is 0.8 V.

gorev.tamam: ε = 0.5 · 0.4 · 4 = 0.8 V. When the rod stops, the area (A) of the circuit no longer changes. The flux stays constant and the current stops.
gorev.ipucu: 0.5 · 0.4 makes 0.2. For 0.8 V you need v = 0.8 / 0.2.

adimlar.metin: Spin the coil at different speeds and watch the voltage on the graph.

gorev.soru: What happens when the coil spins twice as fast?

secenekler.neden: The peaks on the graph get higher too. Since εmax = N·B·A·ω, the peak value increases with the rotation speed.
The waves on the graph also get closer together. Frequency is the number of turns per second.
Since εmax = N·B·A·ω, when the speed doubles the peak value doubles too. The frequency is the number of turns per second, so it doubles as well.

adimlar.metin: In Europe the grid frequency is 50 Hz. So one period lasts T = 1/50 s = 20 ms. Slide the time and find the moment the voltage first reaches its peak value.

gorev.tamam: At T/4 = 5 ms the voltage reaches its peak value of 325 V. The 230 V at the outlet is the rms value: 325 / √2 ≈ 230 V. The voltage reverses twice every period, that is 100 times a second.
gorev.ipucu: The voltage reaches its peak value in a quarter period: 20 / 4.

adimlar.metin: The ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂. The primary coil has 1000 turns and is connected to 230 V. Make the output 11.5 V for a phone charger. Then try the battery too.

gorev.tamam: V₂ = 230 · 50 / 1000 = 11.5 V. When you connect the battery the output is 0, because the flux of a steady current does not change.
gorev.ipucu: 11.5 / 230 makes 1/20. So N₂ must be 1000 / 20.

adimlar.metin: The power plant sends 10 MW, and the resistance of the line is 10 Ω. The power lost as heat in the line is I²·R. Raise the voltage and cut the loss to one hundredth.

gorev.tamam: When the voltage becomes 10 times larger, the current drops to one tenth, and the loss I²·R falls to one hundredth.
gorev.ipucu: The loss is proportional to the square of the current. To cut the current to one tenth, make the voltage 10 times larger.

kapanis: When the flux through a coil changes, an induced voltage forms: ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt. The faster the change, the larger the voltage.
By Lenz's law, the induced current opposes the change that creates it. This is conservation of energy.
A generator produces alternating current: εmax = N·B·A·ω. The grid is 50 Hz. 230 V is the rms value, and about 325 V is the peak value.
For a transformer, V₁ / V₂ = N₁ / N₂. A transformer does not work with direct current.
When the voltage becomes 10 times larger, the transmission loss drops to one hundredth.

yari-iletkenler.ozet: Change resistance by heating, and move charges in doped silicon. Reverse a diode, pick an LED color, and draw current from a solar cell and a transistor. Cool a superconductor and float a magnet in the air.

adimlar.metin: Lower the temperature and watch the two curves.

gorev.soru: Which one's resistance increases as it cools?

secenekler.neden: In cooling silicon the free electrons become fewer, and no charge is left to carry the current. So the resistance increases.
As copper cools, its atoms vibrate less and its resistance decreases.
Look at the curves: one goes down and the other goes up. A metal and a semiconductor behave in opposite ways.

adimlar.baslik: Where does the extra electron go?
adimlar.metin: Phosphorus has been added to silicon. The 5th electron of phosphorus does not go into a bond and is left free. A battery has been connected, making the left end − and the right end +.

gorev.soru: When the battery is connected, which way does the extra electron go?

secenekler.neden: An electron is negatively charged and is attracted to the positive end. The extra electron, free to move in the crystal, carries the current.
Charges of the same sign repel each other. So the electron moves away from the − end.
Since the fifth electron is not in a bond, it is freed easily and moves in the electric field.

adimlar.metin: Now boron has been added instead of phosphorus. Boron comes with 3 electrons, and one bond is left one electron short. This gap is called a hole.

gorev.soru: With the battery connected, which way does the hole go?

secenekler.neden: Neighboring electrons hop into the hole on their way toward the + end. With each hop the hole shifts one step the opposite way, toward the − end. A hole behaves like a positive charge.
The electrons go toward the + end. The hole moves opposite to them.
A hole does not stay put. When a neighboring electron hops into it, the hole moves to that electron's old place.

adimlar.metin: We joined p-type and n-type and got a diode. The plus end of the battery is on the n side, and the voltage is 2.5 V.

gorev.soru: Does the lamp light up?

secenekler.neden: In reverse, the depletion region at the junction thickens and no current flows. If you turn the battery around, the lamp lights up.
In reverse the current is almost zero. So the lamp does not light at all.
The voltage is high, but the direction is wrong. A diode passes current only from p to n.

adimlar.metin: In an LED, as the energy gap grows, the color of the light shifts from red to blue. Change the gap and find the material that gives blue light.

gorev.tamam: The wavelength of blue light is about 450-490 nm, and the energy gap is about 2.5-2.8 eV. It was hard to make a high-quality gallium nitride crystal with such a large gap. That is why the blue LED came last.
gorev.ipucu: The energy gap grows as you go from red to blue.

adimlar.metin: Adjust the irradiance on the panel, that is the light power per square meter (W/m²). Get 150 W of power from a 1 m² panel. The efficiency of the panel is 20%.

gorev.tamam: 0.20 × 750 W/m² × 1 m² = 150 W. At noon on a clear summer day, solar irradiance is about 1000 W/m². This panel gives about 200 W at most.
gorev.ipucu: Power is found with 0.20 × irradiance × 1 m². What is 150 ÷ 0.20?

adimlar.metin: In this classic (BJT) transistor, adjust the base current so that 3 mA flows through the collector. The current is amplified 100 times.

gorev.tamam: 30 µA × 100 = 3000 µA = 3 mA. A small base current controls a current 100 times larger. This is called an amplifier.
gorev.ipucu: 3 mA makes 3000 µA. What is 3000 ÷ 100?

adimlar.metin: A ceramic disk (YBCO) will be cooled with liquid nitrogen. Then a magnet will be lowered over the disk.

gorev.soru: What happens when the magnet comes near the disk?

secenekler.neden: The cooled disk becomes a superconductor and pushes the magnet's field out of its interior. This is called the Meissner effect. The magnet hovers above the disk.
A ceramic is not attracted like iron. In the superconducting state it does the opposite and pushes the field out.
That would happen at room temperature. The cold disk is a superconductor and pushes the field out.

adimlar.metin: Change the temperature and find the highest temperature at which YBCO stays superconducting.

gorev.tamam: YBCO is a superconductor below about 92 K. Liquid nitrogen (77 K) is enough for this, and expensive liquid helium is not needed.
gorev.ipucu: Go just below the point where the green curve drops to zero.

kapanis: The type of dopant decides which charge carries the current. Electrons carry it in n-type, and holes in p-type.
A diode passes current only in the forward direction. The color of an LED is set by its energy gap.
A transistor controls a large current with a small signal (base current or gate voltage).
Below the critical temperature, critical field, and critical current, a superconductor drops to zero resistance and pushes the magnetic field out.

optik.ozet: Enlarge a shadow, bounce a laser onto a target, count images in angled mirrors, find the image in a concave mirror, bend light, catch total internal reflection, and work out color in light and the nearsighted eye.

adimlar.metin: Since light travels along straight lines, a shadow forms behind the ball. The diameter of the ball is 10 cm, and the screen is 120 cm from the lamp. Place the ball so that the diameter of the shadow is exactly 3 times that of the ball. Then try the extended source too.

gorev.tamam: With the point source, the distance from the lamp to the ball is 40 cm and to the screen 120 cm. Since the distance is three times as large, the shadow is three times as large too, that is 30 cm. Similar triangles show this.
gorev.ipucu: The shadow grows by the ratio of the lamp-to-screen distance to the lamp-to-ball distance: 120 / d = 3.

adimlar.metin: In reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Change the angle of the laser and send the reflected ray to the target.

gorev.tamam: The ray that arrived at 40° reflected at 40° on the other side of the normal and hit the target.
gorev.ipucu: The target is at the same height as the laser. The ray goes to the mirror and comes back at the same angle. So the target must be twice as far as the point on the mirror.

adimlar.metin: You joined two mirrors with 60° between them, and a flag stands in between. The images also give images of each other.

gorev.soru: How many images do you see in the mirrors?

secenekler.neden: If the two mirrors gave only one image each, there would be 2 images. But the images are reflected again in the other mirror.
Since 360/α = 6 is an even number, the number of images is n = 360/α − 1 = 5. If the angle between the mirrors were 90°, there would be 3 images.
There are 360/60 = 6 flag positions, but one of them is the object itself. So the number of images is one less.

adimlar.metin: An object stands in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 10 cm. The orange ray comes parallel to the principal axis and passes through the focus (F). The green ray reflects symmetrically at the vertex. Slide the object so that the image is real, inverted, and 2 times larger.

gorev.tamam: The object is between F and C (15 cm). The reflected rays crossed beyond C, and the image was real, inverted, and 2 times larger. You will see how to find this by calculation in Card 11.
gorev.ipucu: The object must be outside F but closer than C. When the object is between F and C, the image is real, inverted, and enlarged.

adimlar.metin: According to Snell's law, n₁·sinθ₁ = n₂·sinθ₂, and in air n = 1. Light arrives from air at 53° (sin 53° ≈ 0.8). Adjust the refractive index of the medium so that the angle of refraction is 30°.

gorev.tamam: Since 1 · 0.8 = n · 0.5, n = 1.6. Light travels in this medium at c/1.6 ≈ 1.9·10⁸ m/s. The larger the index, the more the light bends.
gorev.ipucu: sin 30° = 0.5. Find n from the equation 1 · 0.8 = n · 0.5.

adimlar.metin: A laser sends light to the boundary between two media. Part of the light reflects, and part passes through by refracting. Change the angle of incidence and the refractive index of the lower medium. You can also send the light the other way. Find out the following for yourself.

kontroller.etiket: Send light from the lower medium into air

bulgular.yazi: As light passes from air into glass (n = 1.5), raise the angle of incidence above 80°. Does the light ever fail to get through?
bulgular.tamam: No, the angle of refraction reached about 42° at most. This is the critical angle of glass. Light passing from a smaller index to a larger index always bends toward the normal. There is no total internal reflection in this direction.

bulgular.yazi: Now send the light from glass into air and find an angle at which no light gets out.
bulgular.tamam: When the angle of incidence passed the critical angle (about 42° in glass), all the light reflected back. This is called total internal reflection. This is how a fiber-optic cable traps light.

bulgular.yazi: Make the lower medium diamond (n ≈ 2.42). Find the smallest whole-number angle at which total internal reflection begins.
bulgular.tamam: The critical angle is about 24° in diamond and about 42° in glass. Light entering a diamond is totally reflected many times at the faces and can get out in only a few directions. That is why a diamond sparkles so much.

adimlar.metin: A yellow ball reflects the red and green of white light and absorbs the blue. Now only a red light will be on in the room.

gorev.soru: How does the yellow ball look in red light?

secenekler.neden: For the ball to look yellow, green light must reach the eye along with red. But there is no green light in the room.
The ball reflects red too. It would look black only if there were no light left for it to reflect.
The ball reflects the red light that falls on it. Since no green light arrives, the ball looks only red.

adimlar.metin: The eye works like a converging lens. In a nearsighted eye, rays from far away meet in front of the retina, and distant objects look blurred. Try the two eyeglass lenses one at a time.

gorev.soru: Which eyeglass lens does a nearsighted eye need?

secenekler.neden: A thick-edged lens spreads the rays a little, and the focus shifts back onto the retina.
A thin-edged lens converges the rays even more. So the focus moves even farther from the retina.
A thin-edged lens converges the rays more, and the focus shifts even farther forward of the retina.

kapanis: Light travels along straight lines. A point source makes an umbra, and an extended source makes a penumbra as well.
In reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The angles are measured from the normal.
Two angled mirrors (if 360/α is even) form n = 360/α − 1 images.
For mirrors and lenses, 1/f = 1/d<sub>o</sub> + 1/d<sub>i</sub>. The magnification is found with m = −d<sub>i</sub>/d<sub>o</sub>.
According to Snell's law, n₁·sinθ₁ = n₂·sinθ₂. When light passes from a denser medium to a less dense one, there is total internal reflection if the critical angle is exceeded.
An object appears in the color of the light it reflects. A nearsighted eye gets a thick-edged lens, and a farsighted eye a thin-edged lens.

dalga-optigi.ozet: Pass a wave through a narrow gap and find a fringe in Young's experiment. Work out the path difference, change the fringe spacing, and put the setup under water. Narrow a single slit and block light with a polarizer.

adimlar.metin: A plane wave passes through a gap in a barrier. Narrow the gap and see the wave spread in every direction.

gorev.tamam: When the gap narrows to about one wavelength, a single wavelet source is left there and the wave spreads like a semicircle. This is called diffraction. In a wide gap the common tangent of the wavelets is still a plane front, and the wave bends only a little at the edges.
gorev.ipucu: Diffraction is pronounced when the gap is comparable to the wavelength.

adimlar.metin: At a bright fringe the path difference is a whole multiple of λ. The path difference of the rays reaching P from S₁ and S₂ is Δ = d·x/L. Slide P and find the 2nd bright fringe.

gorev.tamam: At x = 6 mm, Δ = 1200 nm = 2λ. The waves meet crest to crest and interfere constructively. In this setup the fringe spacing is 3 mm. So the 2nd bright fringe is 2 · 3 = 6 mm from the center.
gorev.ipucu: The path difference must be exactly 2 wavelengths: Δ = 1200 nm.

adimlar.metin: If the path difference is a whole multiple of λ a bright fringe forms, and if it is a half multiple a dark fringe forms. Here λ = 500 nm. The light reaching P from S₂ travels 1750 nm farther than the light from S₁.

gorev.soru: What is seen at point P?

secenekler.neden: For a bright fringe, Δ must be a whole multiple of the wavelength. 1750 / 500 = 3.5 is not a whole number.
At the 3rd dark fringe, Δ would be (3 − ½)·λ = 2.5λ = 1250 nm.
Δ/λ = 3.5 = 4 − ½. A crest meets a trough and there is destructive interference. Since the dark fringe condition is Δ = (n − ½)·λ, n = 4.

adimlar.metin: The fringe spacing is found with Δx = λ·L/d. Change the wavelength, the screen distance, and the slit separation. Turn on the light each time and look at the pattern.

gorev.soru: What should you do to bring the fringes closer together?

secenekler.neden: As the slits moved apart, the fringes got closer. You will see the reason in the relation Δx = λL/d on the next card.
Red has a longer wavelength. When λ grows, Δx grows too and the fringes spread apart.
The intensity of the light does not change Δx. The fringes only get brighter.

adimlar.baslik: If the setup is put under water
adimlar.metin: In air the fringe spacing is 4 mm. Now we will immerse the whole setup in water, which has a refractive index of 1.33.

gorev.soru: What happens to the fringes on the screen?

secenekler.neden: In water the wavelength of light becomes 1.33 times smaller. The fringe spacing shrinks by the same ratio: 4 / 1.33 ≈ 3 mm.
For the fringes to spread apart, the wavelength would have to grow. But in water the wavelength shrinks.
Even though the frequency stays the same, Δx = λL/d depends on the wavelength. In water λ shrinks.

adimlar.metin: The width of the central bright fringe is 2λL/w (λ = 500 nm, L = 1 m). Adjust the slit so that the central fringe is 20 mm wide.

gorev.tamam: For w = 50 μm, 2 · 500 nm · 1 m / 50 μm = 20 mm. As the slit narrows, the pattern widens.
gorev.ipucu: The width of the central fringe is inversely proportional to w. To widen the fringe, narrow the slit.

adimlar.metin: A polarizer lets light through only with its vibrations in a single direction. Turn the second polarizer so that no light reaches the screen.

gorev.tamam: When the second polarizer is turned 90° relative to the first, the light is blocked completely. At in-between angles, part of the light gets through.
gorev.ipucu: The transmitted light goes out when the directions of the two polarizers are perpendicular.

kapanis: According to Huygens' principle, every point of a wavefront is a new source. In a narrow gap the wave is diffracted.
Young's experiment shows that light is a wave.
For a bright fringe Δ = n·λ, and for a dark fringe Δ = (n − ½)·λ.
The fringe spacing is found with Δx = λL/d. If the setup is immersed in a liquid, the fringe spacing becomes Δx/n.
In a single slit the width of the central fringe is 2λL/w. When the slit narrows, the pattern widens.
Polarization proves that light is a transverse wave.

ozel-gorelilik.ozet: Add velocities and measure the speed of light. Find the order of the lightning strikes, speed up the light clock and make γ equal 2. Bring the muon to the ground, shorten the ship and push against the c limit.

adimlar.metin: A ball thrown forward from the train moves at 20 m/s relative to the train. What is its speed for an observer on the ground? Speed up the train so that the ball moves at 50 m/s relative to the ground. Then press play.

gorev.tamam: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s. This is how velocities add in classical physics, and it is correct at everyday speeds. So does the light from the train's headlight travel at c + v relative to the ground?
gorev.ipucu: The ball's speed relative to the ground is the train's speed plus 20. The sum must be 50.

adimlar.baslik: The speed of light is c for everyone
adimlar.metin: A ship approaches Earth at 0.5c and turns on its headlight.

gorev.soru: At what speed does an observer on Earth measure the headlight's light?

secenekler.neden: That is what classical velocity addition would say. But the rule fails for light, and measurements always give c.
Measurements always give c. So the speed of light does not add to the motion of the source. Einstein took this as a postulate (next card).
Light does not leave the source slowed down. Both the ship and Earth measure c.

adimlar.metin: Lightning strikes the two ends of a moving train, A and B. The two flashes reach O, standing on the ground exactly in the middle, at the same time. O′, in the middle of the train, is moving toward B. Both flashes travel at c.

gorev.soru: What order of lightning strikes does O′ conclude?

secenekler.yazi: They struck at the same time
secenekler.neden: O′ sees the flashes at different moments and knows both traveled at c. So O′ cannot say the lightning struck at the same time.
O′ is moving away from A. So the light from A reaches O′ later.
O′ moves toward the light ahead and sees it first. Since both flashes travel at c, O′ concludes that B was struck first. Events that are simultaneous in one frame may not be simultaneous in another.

adimlar.baslik: The light clock and time dilation
adimlar.metin: The time a moving observer measures is Δt = γ·Δt₀, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). In the light clock on the ship, light travels straight between two mirrors. Seen from Earth it takes a slanted, longer path, but its speed is still c. 6 years pass on the ship. Set the speed so that 10 years pass on Earth.

gorev.tamam: At 0.8c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 5/3. Δt = γ·Δt0 = 5/3 · 6 = 10 years. The time on the ship, where the events happen at the same place, is the proper time. Proper time is the shortest time, and it is always measured longer from other frames.
gorev.ipucu: γ must be 10 / 6 = 5/3. Since γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), γ grows as you raise v/c.

adimlar.metin: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Set the speed so that the moving clock runs at half speed as seen from Earth, which means γ equals 2.

gorev.ipucu: For γ = 2, √(1 − v²/c²) must be 1/2. Raise the speed a little above 0.8c.

adimlar.baslik: How do muons reach the ground?
adimlar.metin: Cosmic rays produce muons in the atmosphere. The mean lifetime of a muon at rest is 2.2 μs. At 0.995c a muon can travel only 660 m in that time. A muon was born 6.6 km above the ground.

gorev.soru: Can the muon reach the ground within its mean lifetime?

secenekler.neden: At 0.995c, γ is about 10. Seen from the ground, the muon's lifetime is about 22 μs, and in that time it travels about 6.6 km. In the muon's own frame, the atmosphere is γ times thinner, about 660 m.
2.2 μs is the lifetime by the muon's own clock. Seen from the ground, a moving clock runs slow.

secenekler.yazi: Only if it goes faster than light
secenekler.neden: The muon moves at 0.995c. No object with mass can reach c.

adimlar.metin: The ship's length measured in its own frame, its proper length, is 100 m. An observer on Earth measuring the moving ship finds it shorter: L = L0/γ. Set the speed so that the ship measures 60 m.

gorev.tamam: At 0.8c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 5/3 and L = 100 / (5/3) = 60 m. The ship's height stays 20 m. The astronaut on board always measures their own ship as 100 m.
gorev.ipucu: Since 100 / 60 = 5/3, γ must be 5/3. Raise the speed little by little.

adimlar.metin: At high speeds momentum is p = γ·m·v. Give the ship energy step by step and compare Newton's prediction with reality.

gorev.soru: If you keep the engines running without stopping, what happens to the ship's speed?

secenekler.yazi: It passes c after a while
secenekler.neden: That is what Newtonian physics would say. But since γ grows without limit, the speed always stays below c.

secenekler.yazi: It approaches c but never reaches it
secenekler.neden: As v gets close to c, γ grows without limit. The energy needed to speed up a little more also grows without limit.

secenekler.yazi: It reaches exactly c and stays there
secenekler.neden: Reaching c takes infinite energy. So for an object with mass, v < c always.

kapanis: Classical velocity addition works at everyday speeds, but it fails for light. Everyone measures the speed of light as c.
Simultaneity is relative.
Time dilation is found with Δt = γ·Δt₀, where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
Length contracts only along the direction of motion: L = L₀/γ.
An object with mass cannot reach c. Rest energy is E₀ = m·c².
When v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and relativity turns into Newtonian physics.

kuantum.ozet: Heat the object and change its color. Try to eject electrons from a metal, find the stopping voltage and raise the intensity. Scatter an X-ray, send electrons through a double slit and find the color of hydrogen.

adimlar.metin: By Wien's law, λmax·T ≈ 2.9·10⁶ nm·K. Set the temperature so that the peak of the curve is at 500 nm.

gorev.tamam: By Wien's law, λmax = 2.9·10⁶ / 5800 = 500 nm. This is the surface temperature of the Sun.
gorev.ipucu: Since λ<sub>max</sub>·T ≈ 2.9·10⁶ nm·K, T = 2.9·10⁶ / 500.

adimlar.metin: When light falls on a metal, electrons can be ejected. Ejecting an electron from sodium takes at least W = 2.3 eV. Change the color and the intensity, and make at least two different tries.

gorev.soru: What decides whether an electron is ejected?

secenekler.neden: Raising the intensity of red light brings more photons, but each still carries less than 2.3 eV.
An electron absorbs a single photon, and energy does not build up. So waiting below the threshold does not help.
An electron takes the energy of a single photon (h·f). If h·f < W, no electron comes out however intense the light is. For sodium the threshold is about 540 nm.

adimlar.metin: The maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is Ek,max = h·f − W. The photon energy is found with E(eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm), and for sodium W = 2.3 eV. The reverse voltage that stops the fastest electron is called V0: e·V0 = Ek,max. Set the wavelength so that V0 is 0.8 V.

gorev.tamam: At 400 nm the photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Ek,max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV and V0 = 0.8 V.

adimlar.metin: We shine the same 400 nm light on a sodium plate. In the setup on the right the light has twice the intensity, so twice as many photons arrive each second.

gorev.soru: What happens when the intensity doubles?

secenekler.neden: The energy of each photon is h·f. Intensity raises the number of photons, not the energy of a photon.

secenekler.yazi: Current rises, E<sub>k,max</sub> stays the same
secenekler.neden: Twice the photons eject twice the electrons, and the current grows. Each electron still takes the energy of a single photon and comes out with at most 0.8 eV.
The current rises, but the energy of the electrons depends on the energy of a single photon.

adimlar.metin: In 1923 Compton made X-ray photons collide with electrons. A photon has no mass, but it has momentum: p = h/λ. The photon will now hit the electron and scatter.

gorev.soru: What happens to the wavelength of the scattered photon?

secenekler.neden: The photon gives part of its energy to the electron. Its energy drops, λ grows and f gets smaller. The photon's speed is still c.
A shorter wavelength would mean the photon gained energy. But part of the energy goes to the recoiling electron.
Since the electron recoils, it has taken some energy. That energy comes from the photon.

adimlar.metin: de Broglie said that every particle has a wavelength: λ = h/(m·v). Now we send electrons one at a time through two slits to a screen.

gorev.soru: What forms on the screen over time?

secenekler.neden: That would happen if electrons behaved only like tiny balls. But the waves from the two slits interfere.
One by one the dots look random. But when thousands build up, a regular pattern appears.
Each electron lands on the screen as a single dot, which is particle behavior. But as the dots build up, interference fringes appear, which is wave behavior. This is called wave-particle duality.

adimlar.metin: When an electron drops to a lower level, it emits a photon with the energy difference of the two levels. In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV. Find the transition that gives the blue-green photon of 2.55 eV.

gorev.tamam: E4 − E2 = −0.85 − (−3.4) = 2.55 eV and λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ 486 nm. Most transitions down to n = 2 are in the visible range and are called the Balmer series. Those down to n = 1 are in the ultraviolet and are called the Lyman series.
gorev.ipucu: The energies of the levels are −13.6, −3.4, −1.51 and −0.85 eV. Look for the pair whose difference is 2.55.

kapanis: Energy is quantized: E = h·f = h·c/λ. In electronvolts, E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
For a blackbody, the peak wavelength is found with λmax·T ≈ 2.9·10⁻³ m·K.
In the photoelectric effect, Ek,max = h·f − W = e·V₀. Frequency sets the threshold, and intensity changes only the current.
In the Compton effect the photon carries momentum: p = h/λ. The wavelength of the scattered photon gets longer.
The wavelength of a matter wave is found with λ = h/(m·v). Electrons interfere too.
In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV. The emitted photon carries the energy difference between the levels.

radyoaktivite.ozet: Build a nucleus and make an isotope. Weigh the strong force, see the mass defect on a balance and find the most stable nucleus. Go from uranium down to lead, separate the radiations, calculate a half-life and control a chain reaction.

adimlar.metin: This is a carbon-12 nucleus. Turn it into carbon-14.

gorev.tamam: The nucleus has 6 protons and 8 neutrons: 146C. Since Z stayed the same, this is still carbon, and only A changed. So this is an isotope of carbon.
gorev.ipucu: The number of protons decides the element, and for carbon Z must stay 6. Change the number of neutrons to make A = 14.

adimlar.metin: The protons in a nucleus repel each other electrically. The strong nuclear force holds them together. Move the two protons apart (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m) and watch how the two forces change.

gorev.soru: Which is true for the strong nuclear force?

secenekler.neden: The strong force does not depend on charge. It also acts between a proton and a neutron and between two neutrons.

secenekler.yazi: It falls off more slowly with distance than electric repulsion
secenekler.neden: It is the other way around. On the graph the green curve dies out much faster than the red one. At a few fm the strong attraction is almost zero.

secenekler.yazi: It has a very short range
secenekler.neden: At about 1 fm the strong attraction easily beats the repulsion. At a few fm it drops almost to zero. This is why the nucleus is so small.

adimlar.metin: One pan of the balance holds 2 protons and 2 neutrons, all separate. The other pan holds the helium-4 nucleus they form when they join. The parts in the two pans are the same.

gorev.soru: Which side of the balance is heavier?

secenekler.neden: The nucleus is lighter than its parts. The missing mass was released as energy when the nucleus formed.
Mass does not increase when the parts join. On the contrary, part of the mass turns into energy and is released.
The parts are the same, but the masses are not equal. The difference is called the mass defect.

adimlar.metin: If you divide the binding energy by the nucleon number, you see how tightly a nucleus is bound. Change the mass number and find the peak of the curve.

gorev.tamam: The peak is around A ≈ 56-62, where the energy per nucleon is about 8.8 MeV. Iron-56 and nickel-62 are among the most stable nuclei.
gorev.ipucu: The curve rises fast for light nuclei and falls slowly for heavy ones. Look for the highest point in between.

adimlar.metin: α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ decay raises Z by 1. <sup>238</sup>U decays step by step down to stable <sup>206</sup>Pb. How many α and how many β⁻ does this take?

gorev.tamam: The difference in A is 238 − 206 = 32. Since only α changes A, it takes 32 / 4 = 8 α. 8 α lower Z by 16, down to 76. For Z to rise to 82, it takes 6 β⁻.
gorev.ipucu: First find the number of α from the difference in A: 238 − 206 = 32. Then fix Z with β⁻.

adimlar.metin: A source gives off α, β⁻ and γ radiation. The radiations will pass first between two charged plates, then through sheets of paper, aluminum and lead.

gorev.soru: Which is deflected most in the electric field?

secenekler.neden: α has a double charge, but it is very heavy, because it is a helium nucleus. So it bends only a little toward the negative plate.
β⁻ is an electron. Its charge-to-mass ratio is thousands of times that of α, so it bends the most, toward the positive plate. Uncharged γ does not bend at all.
γ is an uncharged photon. So it does not bend at all in an electric field.

adimlar.metin: How long must you wait for 15 g to be left from 120 g of a substance with a half-life of 4 days?

gorev.tamam: The amount goes from 120 to 60, to 30 and to 15. That is three half-lives, or 12 days.
gorev.ipucu: How many times must you halve 120 to get 15? Each halving takes 4 days.

adimlar.metin: In a power plant, control rods absorb the extra neutrons. How many neutrons from each fission must cause a new fission for the reaction to go on at a steady rate?

gorev.tamam: If each fission starts exactly one new fission, the reaction goes on at a steady rate. This is how nuclear power plants work. If the number is 2 or 3, the number of fissions multiplies with each generation and the reaction gets out of control. If it is 0, the reaction dies out.
gorev.ipucu: The number of fissions must stay the same from one generation to the next.

kapanis: Z is the number of protons and decides the element. A = Z + N. Nuclei with the same Z but different A are called isotopes.
The strong nuclear force does not depend on charge and has a very short range.
A nucleus is lighter than its parts, and the difference corresponds to an energy of E = Δm·c². Binding energy per nucleon is greatest around iron.
α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ raises Z by 1, and β⁺ lowers Z by 1. In γ emission A and Z do not change.
In an electric field β⁻ is deflected most, and γ is not deflected. The order of penetration is γ > β > α.
The amount left is found with N = N₀ / 2ⁿ. Fission splits a nucleus, and fusion joins nuclei. Both release energy.

simya.baslik: The science of chemistry: from alchemy to chemistry
simya.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Distill a mixture, split water and weigh a closed flask.

adimlar.metin: The alchemists' biggest goal was to turn lead into gold. Today we know the difference. A lead atom has 82 protons in its nucleus, and a gold atom has 79.

gorev.soru: Why did lead never turn into gold?

secenekler.yazi: Reactions do not change proton number
secenekler.neden: In a chemical reaction only electrons and bonds change. To turn lead into gold you would have to remove 3 protons from the nucleus. Only a nuclear reaction can do that, and only in tiny amounts.

secenekler.yazi: They could not heat it enough
secenekler.neden: A furnace's heat breaks bonds, but it does not reach the nucleus. Even the hottest furnace cannot change the number of protons.

secenekler.yazi: They never found the philosopher's stone
secenekler.neden: The problem was not a missing ingredient but the type of reaction. No substance can change the number of protons by chemical means.

adimlar.metin: The flask holds a mixture of water and alcohol. What happens when you heat it?

gorev.soru: When you heat it, which reaches the collecting flask first?

secenekler.neden: Alcohol boils at about 78 °C and water at 100 °C. So the alcohol evaporates and condenses first. The collected liquid still contains some water, so distillation is repeated to get pure alcohol.
Water boils at 100 °C, so it evaporates later than alcohol.
Their boiling points differ, so one evaporates first.

adimlar.metin: Since ancient times water was thought to be an element. Is it really? Pass an electric current through water (this experiment was first done in 1800).

gorev.soru: What happens to the water when the current is on?

secenekler.yazi: It splits into two different gases
secenekler.neden: Hydrogen collects at the negative pole and oxygen at the positive pole. The volume of hydrogen is twice that of oxygen. This is the 2 to 1 ratio in the formula H₂O.
The electric current breaks the water down, and gas collects in the tubes.
This is decomposition, not evaporation. The gases in the tubes are hydrogen and oxygen, not water vapor.

adimlar.metin: Robert Boyle proposed a definition in 1661. By this definition, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances. Look at what collected in the tubes.

gorev.soru: By this definition, what is water?

secenekler.neden: Water split into two simpler substances, so it cannot be an element. Water is a compound in which hydrogen and oxygen combine in a fixed ratio.
That was the old idea, but the experiment showed that water breaks down. In science, the experiment has the last word.
The gases were not dissolved in the water. They separated only through a chemical change, and always in a 2 to 1 ratio. This shows that water is a compound.

adimlar.metin: You will heat tin in a sealed flask. The tin will slowly turn into a white powder.

gorev.soru: When the heating is done, what does the balance show?

secenekler.neden: Nothing enters or leaves the sealed flask. The atoms only rearrange, and the total mass stays the same. This is called conservation of mass.
The tin gets heavier, but the oxygen it needs comes from the air inside the flask. The total does not change.
Nothing can escape from a sealed flask, so the mass cannot go down.

adimlar.metin: Now leave the flask open and repeat the experiment. Watch the balance.

gorev.tamam: The mass went up! The tin combined with oxygen from the air. Nothing escaped from the flask. New air came in from outside to replace the oxygen used up.

adimlar.metin: A chemist says that when a metal burns, phlogiston leaves it, so the metal gets lighter. How would you test this claim with the scientific method?

gorev.soru: Which one really tests the claim?

secenekler.yazi: Burn it in a closed container and weigh
secenekler.neden: Measurement tests the claim. When tin burned its mass went up, so nothing came out of it. Oxygen went in from the air. This is how the phlogiston idea fell apart.
In science, evidence counts, not authority. Famous scholars can be wrong too.
Books repeat a claim but do not test it. Testing needs experiment and measurement.

kapanis: Alchemy searched for gold and the elixir of life, but failed. That is because chemical reactions do not change an element.
Alchemy left behind distillation and lab equipment. Distillation separates by boiling point difference.
For Boyle, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances. Water can be broken down, so it is a compound.
Lavoisier showed that in a closed container the total mass before and after a reaction is the same. This is called conservation of mass.
Repeatable experiments and measurement, in other words the scientific method, made chemistry a science.

kimya-bilimi.baslik: The language and safety of chemistry
kimya-bilimi.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Build formulas, decode symbols and recognize hazard symbols.

adimlar.metin: Add atoms to build water, H₂O.

gorev.tamam: Two hydrogens and one oxygen combine to form H₂O. The subscript of oxygen is 1, so it is not written. The water molecule is bent, not straight.

adimlar.metin: This molecule is CO, carbon monoxide, a toxic gas. Add one more oxygen to make the CO₂ you breathe out.

gorev.tamam: CO₂ is called carbon dioxide. A single oxygen completely changes the substance. CO sticks to the hemoglobin in blood and blocks oxygen transport. CO₂ is already in the air you breathe.

adimlar.metin: Some symbols come from the element's Latin name. For example, the symbol for iron is Fe (ferrum) and for gold Au (aurum). Decode this symbol.

gorev.soru: Sn is the symbol for which element?

secenekler.neden: Sn comes from stannum, the Latin name for tin. A food can is steel with a thin coating of tin.
The symbol for sodium is Na, from its Latin name natrium.
The symbol for silicon is Si. Sn comes from the Latin name stannum.

adimlar.metin: Now build table salt, NaCl.

gorev.tamam: NaCl is called sodium chloride, which is table salt. Salt is actually a crystal made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The formula shows their 1 to 1 ratio.

adimlar.metin: Look at the symbol on the label before you open the bottle.

gorev.soru: What does this symbol mean?

secenekler.neden: The flame symbol marks flammable substances such as alcohol, acetone and gasoline. They are kept away from flames and sparks.
The explosive symbol shows an exploding bomb.
A toxic substance is marked with a skull.

adimlar.metin: This symbol looks like the first one, but there is a circle under the flame. This small difference means a very different hazard.

gorev.soru: Which kind of substance does this symbol mark?

secenekler.neden: The flame over a circle marks substances that do not burn themselves but give off oxygen and start or intensify burning. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is an example. These are kept away from flammable substances.
The flammable symbol shows only a flame, with no circle under it.
The corrosive symbol shows liquid dripping onto a hand and a surface and eating them away.

adimlar.metin: You need to dilute a concentrated acid. A lot of heat is released when acid and water mix.

gorev.soru: How do you mix them?

secenekler.yazi: Add the acid slowly to water
secenekler.neden: When acid is added a little at a time to plenty of water, the heat spreads through the large mass of water and nothing splashes. That is why acid is always added to water.
A little water on top of the acid heats up suddenly, boils and splashes the acid.
It does matter, because if water is added to acid, the hot water can splash the acid.

kapanis: In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase. Co is cobalt, while CO is carbon monoxide.
The subscript in a formula shows how many of that atom there are. A subscript of 1 is not written (H₂O, CO₂).
Some symbols come from Latin names. Fe comes from ferrum, Au from aurum and Pb from plumbum.
Diamond-shaped symbols with a red border describe hazards. A flame marks a flammable substance, and a flame over a circle marks an oxidizing substance.
When diluting, add acid to water slowly, never the other way around.

madde.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Heat water, watch the particles, mix substances and burn one.

adimlar.metin: The container holds water particles. Change the temperature and see how the particles are arranged. Then turn the water into a gas.

gorev.tamam: In a gas the particles are far apart and fast, and they fill the whole container. In a solid they vibrate in place, and in a liquid they slide past each other. The particles are always the same water molecules. Only their arrangement and motion change.

adimlar.metin: You keep heating the ice and measure its temperature. The graph will show how the temperature changes over time.

gorev.soru: While the ice melts, it keeps absorbing heat. What happens to its temperature?

secenekler.neden: The heat absorbed goes into pulling the particles apart. So the temperature stays at 0 °C while melting and at 100 °C while boiling (at 1 atm). Mixtures, on the other hand, usually melt over a range of temperatures.
The ice absorbs heat, but its temperature does not rise while it melts. The heat goes into something else.
The ice is absorbing heat, not releasing it. So its temperature does not drop.

adimlar.metin: Look at the particles in the boxes. If different atoms are bonded in a fixed ratio, it is a compound. If substances sit together without bonding, it is a mixture.

gorev.soru: Which box holds a compound?

secenekler.neden: These molecules have two atoms, but both are oxygen. It contains only one kind of atom, so this substance is an element: O₂.
In each molecule two hydrogens are bonded to one oxygen, so this substance is water (H₂O). Different atoms are bonded in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound.
Here H₂ and O₂ molecules sit together without bonding. So this is a mixture of two elements.

adimlar.metin: You will stir both glasses well. One has sugar and water, the other olive oil and water.

gorev.soru: After stirring and waiting, which one is the same everywhere?

secenekler.neden: Sugar dissolves in water and spreads evenly everywhere. Olive oil does not dissolve, and since it is less dense than water it rises to the top, forming two layers.
Oil and water do not mix. After waiting, the oil collects on top.
Stirring does not dissolve everything. After waiting, one of the glasses separates into layers.

adimlar.metin: What changes when ice melts? Watch the water molecules up close.

gorev.soru: What happens to the water molecules when ice melts?

secenekler.neden: Melting is a physical change. The molecule is still H₂O, and the substance is still water. Tearing paper and dissolving sugar are also physical changes.

secenekler.yazi: They split into H and O atoms
secenekler.neden: Splitting water into its atoms takes a chemical method such as electrolysis. Melting does not do that.
Melted ice is still water. If you freeze it, it becomes ice again.

adimlar.metin: Now you are burning charcoal, which is carbon. The carbon atoms will meet oxygen molecules from the air.

gorev.soru: What happens when carbon burns?

secenekler.neden: Carbon and oxygen bond to form carbon dioxide (CO₂), and this is a chemical change. The atoms do not disappear. They bond in a new arrangement. Heat and light given off are also clues of a chemical change.

secenekler.yazi: It only turns into a gas
secenekler.neden: If only the state changed, the molecule would stay the same. Here carbon combines with oxygen to form a new substance.
Atoms do not disappear in a reaction. They only bond again with other atoms.

kapanis: Matter is anything with mass and volume. In a solid the particles are ordered and vibrate, in a liquid they slide past each other, and in a gas they are far apart and fast.
A pure substance has a definite melting and boiling point. While the state is changing, the temperature stays constant. Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at 1 atm.
An element is made of one kind of atom, and a compound of different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio. In a mixture the substances do not bond to each other.
A homogeneous mixture is the same everywhere, for example sugar water. In a heterogeneous mixture you can tell the parts apart, for example olive oil and water.
In a physical change the substance stays the same, as in melting and dissolving. In a chemical change a new substance forms, as in burning and rusting.
